lines.text: Lecture 1
The goal of the Alcibiades according to Proclus: seven supporting arguments
Now then, the target (skopos) of the present dialogue, according to Proclus, is self-knowledge: and this is confirmed by a plurality of arguments.

5 First by the title: for the dialogue is entitled the ‘Greater Alcibiades, or On the Nature of a Human Being’. (It is ‘greater’ since there is another ‘lesser’ Alcibiades by Plato, just as there is a ‘greater’ and a ‘lesser’ Hippias).
Next on the basis of certain expressions in the dialogue; for example, it is stated in it ‘But, my good 10 friend, being persuaded by me and by the inscription at Delphi, “Know Thyself”. ’

And in addition in the dialogue before us the following three designations are distinguished: ‘me’, ‘what belongs to me’, and ‘what belongs to my belongings’. And from the statement that all who were in love with the body of Alcibiades did not love Alcibiades , but rather one of his 15 possessions, and it was Socrates alone who loved Alcibiades himself.

Furthermore from the assertion that the just and the advantageous are in this work interchangeable, from which it is clear that this discussion is about the soul: for to alone is the just advantageous, since it is not advantageous to the composite : for example, the death of Menoeceus was just, since he died on behalf of his fatherland, but it was not advantageous to the body that perished.

And from the fact that concludes the discussion once he has demonstrated, at the end of the dialogue, that the human being is the soul, on the ground that all of the prior assumptions are made for the purpose of establishing this .

5 And also because Socrates strives not only to lead his beloved (paidika) upwards, but to do so along the very path by which he has himself been led upwards: for it is reported that he came to philosophy from the Pythian inscription, ‘Know Thyself’.

And, further, from the use in the work of the following expression – ‘self’, ‘the self itself.’ Now Proclus takes this one way, and Damascius another. For Proclus says that ‘self’ is the tripartite soul (hê trimereia tês psukhês), or simply the soul, and that ‘the self itself’ is the rational soul: but Damascius approaches this differently and says that ‘self’ is the rational soul, while ‘the self itself’ the highest and most intellectual part of the soul.
This is the goal according to Proclus.
The target of the Alcibiades according to Damasciu s

But Damascius conveys its goal more exactly and more truly when he says that it is not about knowing oneself unqualifiedly, but about knowing oneself as a civic person (politikôs). And he establishes this from the definition of the human being in this dialogue as a rational soul (psukhê logikê) that uses the body as an instrument. Only the civic person uses the body as an instrument, 20 since he is sometimes in need of spirited emotion (thumos), for example on behalf of his country, but also of an appetite (epithumia) for doing his citizens good. But neither the purificatory person (kathartikos) nor the contemplative person (theôrêtikos) need the body. For a purificatory person is 5,1 the soul freeing itself from the body, though the ‘chains’ nevertheless remain and are not released as from the Ambracian youth; instead, they are released through sympathy. For it is possible for beings even here to exist above in a contemplative manner, because of a certain kind of sympathy, and also for 5 beings above to exist here, when the soul sheds its wings, descends here and becomes aflutter about , because of its love of the body. And the contemplative person is a soul that has been released from the body, while again here we become intellectually aware (noein) of a release on account of the independence . For the soul of the contemplative person, by being active (energousa) in accordance with that which is most divine within it, is in this way freed from its shell-like, pneumatic vehicle. And on this subject the Poet says
Adroit Odysseus then stripped off his rags...
In other words, the contemplative person who has separated himself from such ‘rags’ is truly ‘adroit’ (polumêtis).

So, then, the target of the dialogue concerns knowing oneself as a civic person, if indeed the body is an impediment to the purificatory and contemplative person, and the pure person (kathartikos) is distinguished by 15 moderation of the passions (metriopatheia), and the contemplative one (theôrêtikos) by freedom from them (apatheia). That is Damascius’ position.
The target of the Alcibiades according to the commentators: a reconciliation of the views of Proclus and Damascius

Now if it is necessary for us, who plead Proclus’ cause, to bring Damascius into agreement with him, then does say that the target is civic self-knowledge primarily (proêgoumenôs), . And we should explain this in a plausible way. For when Socrates was watching Alcibiades ‘dashing into civic life (ta politika)’ he realised that he would not readily tolerate questioning about knowledge of his soul (i.e. himself), unless also discussed his present appetite. 5 This is what the Platonic philosophy is like, and in this it possesses a great superiority over the other : for Socrates’ admonishments are like painless purifications, or medicines drenched in honey. For does not heal (epanorthoun) souls by the opposites , as Hippocrates prescribes for bodies when he says ‘opposites are cures for opposites’; nor in the way that Aristotle exhorts us to check spirited emotion (thumos) with appetite (epithumia), and appetite with spirited emotion, inasmuch as these are opposites; nor as the Pythagoreans do, through the ‘tasting’ of the passions, i.e. ‘with the tip of the finger’, as they put it: for one could never heal the person who is aflame with the passions, they say, without some small concession to them. (And this is also why in the Poet , Athena is depicted as urging Pandarus to break his oath, on 7,1 the ground that he is painfully eager to do so – for if we reasoned otherwise, it would be very strange to suppose that the god was issuing a summons to wrongdoing – and this is why the Poet also depicts being punished through his tongue, into that with which he broke his oath.)

And so Socrates does not heal souls in this way, like those we have just 5 mentioned, but rather by that are similar : if someone is a lover, by saying ‘learn what the love of beautiful things is’; if one is a lover of wealth, we say ‘learn what self-suffi ciency is’; if one is a lover of pleasure, ‘learn what the easy life truly is, which the Poet even attributes to the gods by speaking of “the gods who live at ease”. ’ Therefore Socrates, by also being such to Alcibiades, converses with 10 him about civic self-knowledge, and incorporates about purificatory and contemplative . For he says in the present work, ‘Just as, if the Demiurge had told the eye, “Look at yourself”, it would have been unable to do so on account of its not being self-moving, but would have looked at another eye, and not at any random part of it, but at the one entrusted (empepisteumenon) with optical activity (which is also called 8,1 the “pupil” (korê), because of the appearance of little images in it), so too should you, Alcibiades, since you have blinded the self-moving in you by giving yourself over to non-rational activities, look away to me – that is, to the soul of Socrates – and not to any random part of this, but to the highest part, and you shall see in me intellect and god.’

Now by saying ‘look away to me’, he has indicated that the target of the dialogue is self-knowledge in a civic sense; and by saying ‘not to any random part,’ that it is also in a purificatory sense, for self-purification is the province of the highest part of the soul; and by saying ‘you shall see in me intellect’, that it is also in a contemplative sense, for engaging with the realities in accordance with his intellect befits the 10 contemplative; and through saying ‘and god’, that it is also in an inspired sense, for we are inspired according to the divine in us, which is simple, just as is the divine itself. After all, it is through being independent and simple that children and country-dwellers experience inspiration to a greater degree: inspiration cannot be captured by imagination (aphantasiastos), which is why it is undone by imagination, because that is its opposite.

15 And since we have mentioned the Delphic inscription, ‘Know Thyself’, it should be realised that it was not inscribed before the inner shrine to no purpose, but since it beheld everyone as they arrived – whether they came to inquire about their children, like Laius, or about offi ces of state, like Cylon, or about wars, like Croesus, while, in line with that Megarian saying, leaving oneself out of the reckoning – it was therefore set in writing that they 20 think about themselves and get to know themselves first, and the other things subsequently.

9,1 And through the injunction, revealed what was enjoined: that the human being is the rational soul. For says ‘Know Thyself’, and this was addressed to the soul, which has a capacity for knowledge (gnôstikos). Consider that the body does not gain knowledge, nor does the combination in respect of the body. Nor does the vegetative come to know.

But someone might object that even if this does not 5 , still the non-rational soul does. But the inscription is not discussing this , for it adds on ‘Thyself’, whereas the non-rational soul cannot get to know itself, since it cannot revert upon itself, but only the rational soul does that. Yet the heavenly also have knowledge, and indeed know themselves, since they turn back . But the phrase ‘Know Thyself’ does not apply to them either, for in saying ‘Know’, 10 speaks of being transformed from ignorance to knowledge, namely a fulfilment (teleiotês) for the soul, whereas those always know . So it is speaking only with reference to the rational soul.

Equivalent, then, to this inscription at Apollo’s are the mirrors in Egyptian temples, since they are set up before the holy places and possess the same power as the Pythian inscription (for they set them up for self-knowledge, 15 since always indicate realities through riddles, just as the Greeks do through written words).

And again, what the first treatise (kephalaion) in the Enneads is for Plotinus – What is the Living Being and What is the Human Being , in which demonstrates that the combination is a living being (zôion) and the soul a human being (anthrôpos) – that is what the Alcibiades is for Plato, and it has the same kind of target.
That is the content of the lecture (praxis).
Lecture 2
With the god’s favour
Soc. Son of Clinias, I think that you are wondering...

After the target, which is threefold – including the views adopted by Proclus, by Damascius, and by the commentators (i.e. the view shared by the commentators) – come, let us also get into detail about the usefulness (to khrêsimon) of the present dialogue, which is also threefold.
The usefulness (khrêsimon) of the dialogue

10,1 For us, the present dialogue contributes in the first place to the soul’s immortality (athanasia) and everlasting nature (aïdion); and this follows naturally. For if is discussing the process of getting to know oneself in this , and it is by reverting upon ourselves that we get to know ourselves, and the philosophers have demonstrated in countless treatises that everything which reverts upon itself is eternal and immortal, then here we shall get to know that the soul is immortal.

Second, it also contributes to our knowledge (gnôsis) of all beings (panta ta onta): for if we know the soul, we shall also know the formulas (logoi) that it holds within itself; and it holds the formulas of all beings and their patterns 10 (tupoi), since it serves as their image (indalma); and therefore the knowledge of the soul contributes for us to the of all beings.

Third, to knowing what is good for the soul and what is harmful to it. For consider that if the human being (anthrôpos) happened to be a body, it would find fulfilment (teleiotês) in size and beauty; and if it happened to be spirited emotion (thumos), in the love of honour; and if it happened to be appetite (epithumia), in the love of pleasure: by the same token, since it is reason (logos), i.e. the rational soul (logikê psukhê), excellence of character (aretê) is solely suffi cient for its well-being (eudaimonia), while defectiveness of character (kakia) for its ill-being (kakodaimonia). For, as Plato says, the soul shall go forth into the next world possessing nothing except its excellence and defect of character.
So much for the usefulness .
The position (taxis) of the dialogue

As for its position (taxis) , it should be said that must come first in order of all the Platonic . For as says in the Phaedrus, it is laughable for someone who is in a rush to know 11,1 everything else to remain ignorant of himself. Secondly, since it is necessary to learn the of Socrates in a Socratic way, and Socrates reportedly came to philosophy from the ‘Know Thyself’. Also, one should consider that this dialogue is similar to the fore-gates , and just as those lead on to the Holy of Holies 5 (aduton), so one should liken the Alcibiades to the fore-gates, and the Parmenides to the Holy of Holies.
The division (diairesis) of the dialogue

As for the division (diairesis) into sections (kephalaia), it should be recognised that this dialogue is divided into three: refutation (elenktikon), of exhortation (protreptikon), and of midwifery (maieutikon).

In the of refutation , demonstrates that is doubly uneducated: both because he is ignorant of civic affairs (ta politika), and because he thinks that he does understand them. For he is 10 ignorant because he has neither learned from a teacher nor inquired into (zêtêsas) by himself. because knowledge arises in two ways, either by the learning which comes through teachers (didaskaloi), or by inquiry on our own part: and it is better to know by inquiring oneself than by learning from someone else, considering that the self-moving is also superior to that which is moved by another (as Aristotle says in the Rhetorical Arts), and the self-originated (autophuês) to that which is taught by another. Thus he demonstrates that Alcibiades, as we have explained, does not understand civic affairs (ta politika) in even one of these ways. For he did not study under teachers: he learned only reading and writing, music, and wrestling, and moreover there was clearly never a time when, considering himself to be ignorant, he approached a teacher (for even when he was a child and very young, when playing dice he used to say to the others, swearing an 20 oath, that ‘I’m being cheated!’ (adikoumai), as though he knew exactly what was just (dikaios): nor, clearly, did he inquire . As a result, he did not know the goal (telos) of the civic person from these – namely, the just, the advantageous (sumpheron), and even the beautiful. So much for the of refutation.

12,1 The of exhortation is the one in which Socrates exhorts him to conquer his antagonists by wisdom (sophia), for it was an ancestral tradition among the Athenians to conquer by wisdom. (The enemies of the Athenians were the Lacedaimonians and the Persians, as the Peloponnesian and Persian demonstrate).

5 The of midwifery is the one in which Socrates, through a line of questioning appropriate to nature, makes Alcibiades prove that the human being is the soul, so that he himself is his own teacher: here, then, is the doctrine (dogma) that the answerer is the speaker. For this is the sort of person that Socrates is, acting as midwife to souls for the birth of ideas (logoi): which is also why they say that he is the son of Phainarete, who was a midwife (maia) – like Hermes . For just as the doctor merely removes discharges from eyes, and impediments to the functioning of vision, and just as midwives bring babies into the light but do not put them into the persons who give birth, similarly Socrates acts as a midwife for souls (psukhai), and does not put theories into the young, as though into lifeless (apsukhos) vessels. As a matter of fact, he 15 himself says in the Theaetetus that ‘the god has made me act as midwife, and prevents me from producing’.

Then at the end of the dialogue he finishes by exchanging their roles (to skhêma tês tukhês), and makes himself, who was previously the lover, the beloved and Alcibiades, who was previously the beloved, the lover. For this is the goal of the art of love, namely, the reciprocation of love. And Socrates has 20 a lover’s disposition (erôtikos), as he also says in the Phaedrus to Love (Erôs): 13,1 ‘that art of love which you gave me, Master, please do not take away from me, nor disable through some anger or other cause’. Alexander too, after seeing a certain army in a miserable state, reportedly said, ‘May the man who put so many in this condition come to a bad end (apoloito kakista)’. At the end, too, 5 concludes the dialogue by comparing his love to the storks: since the storks too, having first been nourished by their parents, finally nourish them in their old age, and in this way they change .
That is the content of the lecture.
Lecture 3
With the god’s favour
10Soc. Son of Clinias, I think that you are wondering why I, who was the first person to become your lover, am the only one who doesn’t abandon now that the others have left off, .
Because the dialogue is about love (erôtikos), uses the proem to explain three differences between the divinely inspired (entheos) lover and the crude (phortikos) lover.
The differences between the crude and divine lovers

The first difference is that the crude lover wonders at his beloved (ta paidika), whereas the divinely inspired lover is the object of wonder. And 15 illustrates this in the words, ‘Son of Clinias, I think that you are wondering...’ – that is, ‘at me’.

The second difference is that the crude lover coordinates his passion with the bloom of youth and soon abandons his beloved, whereas the divinely inspired lover accompanies his beloved from swaddling-clothes to grave, provided that the physiognomic signs of the begotten declare him worthy of love. And makes this clear when he says, ‘I, who was the first man to become your lover, am the only one who doesn’t abandon you now that the others have left off ’, indicating that he follows his beloved before they do, alongside them, and after them.

And the third difference is that the divinely inspired lover is present (sunesti) with his beloved in a godlike way (theoeidôs), that is, without physical presence: 14,1 for just as the radiance of the divine (to theion) is present in every place, yet its essence (ousia) is in no place (since it is not confined in place), the divinely inspired lover is present in a way that imitates this same mode . But the crude lover is present with his beloved when he wants to engage 5 in acts (energein) at the level of bodily sensation, at the lowest level at that, namely, touch. He has made this clear in his statement, ‘Since the others mobbed you, but I didn’t say a word over so many years’ , showing that he is absent insofar as he is silent, but present insofar as he follows and loves .

These are the differences here, but also presents a fourth difference of the same kind (toiautên) in the Phaedrus: namely, that the presence of the crude lover injures the beloved, in body and soul and outward : in body, because wants to make him effeminate and unmanly; in soul, since he wishes him to be unintelligent (anoêton), with a view to making him suggestible about doing what wants; in outward , since he also to be poor, so that he is dependent on 15 and willing him with pleasures. In fact, he even wants him to be fatherless, motherless, and unloved, so that he has no one to keep him from his company. But the divinely inspired lover is not like this. He is present, not for these kinds of reasons, but the good for his beloved, by reverting to fine and beautiful things (ta kala).

20 Since, then, we have learned the differences between the inspired lover and the crude lover, we should examine why they are called by one and the same name in spite of the stark differentiation and opposition between them, and not as the opposites are – for example, ‘moderation’ (sôphrosunê) and ‘indulgence’ (akolasia). Well, we reply that Love, thanks to the superabundance of his power, has been able to shape even opposites for his own purposes. For ‘all love is madness straining’, insofar as both want to ‘give birth in beauty’ – the inspired to learning in the soul, and the crude to living beings in the body.
The daimoniccause of Socrates’ presence and the order of daimons

But says that the cause of his godlike presence, and of his not 15,1 speaking to until now, ‘is not human’, but is ‘some daimonic opposition’ ; and this makes sense. For if the effect (namely, the godlike presence) is more than human, surely the cause of the presence is divine to a much greater degree.

5 Because the ‘daimonic’ was mentioned in this passage, the commentators have been obliged to pay close attention to the theory (logos) of daimons. It should be understood that there are three divisions (diaphorai) of daimons, because some are daimons by analogy (kat’ analogian), others by essence (kat’ ousian), and others by relation (kata skhesin).

Now those that are essentially daimonic are really the standards (gnômones) for those that are analogically and relatively so, because those that are superior 10 to essential daimons are daimonic in an analogical sense, while those that are inferior to them are by relation .

analogical are so called because, inasmuch as these are primary, they possess the formulas (logoi) of the essential daimons: in other words, they are daimons in a causal way (kat’ aitian), because what causally is necessarily prior to what existently. The orator Isocrates also demonstrates that these are called daimons, 15 when he says, ‘honour the daimonic, always, and especially when the city does’; and Homer ‘ into the midst of the other daimons’ ; and Orpheus portrays Zeus as saying to his own father,
Make straight our race, glorious daimon.
For in these cases, the name ‘daimon’ is bestowed on the divine.

16,1 The souls of those who have lived well are called ‘daimons’ by relation – for instance, the souls of the golden race, which depend upon (skhetikôs ekhousai) daimons, and which are themselves addressed as ‘daimons’. Thus Hesiod, too, says about them:
They are called holy daimons dwelling upon the earth (epikhthonioi), 5 noble, warders-off of evil, guardians of mortal humans.
As we said, then, the name ‘daimon’ is threefold.

We should also investigate how they arrived at the concept (ennoia) of claiming that daimons exist. We assert, then, the following: Our soul, which streams with life and bubbles over with it, is unable to
exist without engendering life (zôopoiein).
(a) For there are times when is inactive with respect to its
cognitive (kata tas gnôstikas), for example when it is
10 overcome by lethargy, but this is never the case with respect to the
life-engendering . The ovoid (ôioeidês) or luminous (augoeides) vehicle was invented
(epenoêthê) for when the shell-form (ostreïnos) body
was not always attached to it. This vehicle has two names:
(a) ‘ovoid’ on account of its shape (skhêma), for it is not
altogether spherical like the heavenly , but less spherical
, and for this reason they say that it sometimes suffers
17,1 ‘distortion’ (diastrophên), but certainly isn’t destroyed; because it is of
the same essence (ousia) as the heavenly bodies, that is, of the fift h
body, and therefore also everlasting (aïdios);
(b) it is called ‘luminous’ from its essence (ousia), because it is
transparent and aetherial. Just as they assigned this luminous vehicle to the soul, in order that,
5 being fastened all through it (dia pantos), it might always engender life,
in the same way, in the case of the heavenly bodies, which cannot cease
from activity (energein), they fastened this essentially daimonic race to
them. (For our souls are not always fastened to them on account of our
shedding our feathers and descending into becoming). This , then, being intermediary, is the interpreter for

here of from the gods. 10 But since interprets every attribute of the heavenly beings, because there are six things in the heavenly beings, it – I mean the race of essential daimons – has also been divided into six. In the heavenly beings, then, are : Divinity (theotês), Mind (nous), Rational Soul (psukhê logikê), Non-Rational Soul (psukhê alogos), Form (eidos), and Matter (hulê), therefore the different types of daimons are equal in number. 18,1 Those who link us to the Divinity of the heavenly are called ‘divine’ (theioi), who preside over (ephestêkasin) inspirations.

Those who link us to the Mind are called ‘intellective’ (noêroi): they preside over common concepts (koinai ennoiai), by means of which, beyond demonstration, we know certain among the common concepts even without demonstration (anapodeiktôs).
5 Those that to the Rational Soul are called ‘psychic’. Concerning them, the poet says,
And a daimon will advise you on the rest,
and
First a daimon breathed it in my mind, a great web.
10 Those that link us to the Non-Rational of the heavenly beings ‘non-rational’ (alogoi).

Those to the Form of the heavenly are called ‘formal’ or ‘form-like’. That our forms are linked to the forms of the heavenly, is clear from their growing and shrinking along with the heavenly , for the 15 humours wax and wane with the moon (selênê), and so do hairs, for which reason we see that those who live a priestly life do not cut their hair while the moon is waxing. And epilepsy (to selêniakos pathos) also makes this clear, and 19,1 heliotropic plants, and moon-stones too, by waxing and waning with the moon; and similarly oysters, and just about everything. For this reason, this saying was well addressed to the moon:
You build everything up when you are waxing, and crush everything when you are waning.

Next, the who fasten this matter here to the matter of the heavenly are called ‘material’. Since they stand guard over 5 by doing this, they do not allow it to be utterly destroyed, although it is in a state of flux (rheustos). For Orpheus, too, speaks
of matter heavenly, starry, and boundless deep,

on the basis that matter is threefold and that one kind, which functions as the substrate for the seven spheres, is ‘heavenly’; another, which functions as that for the stars, ‘starry’; and , which he has called ‘boundless deep’ 10 (abussos) because it is lowest (eskhatos) and in flux, earthly (khthonios).

But since we have stated that the first form in the heavenly is the divine (to theion), we must understand that among the gods, some are beyond the cosmos (huperkosmioi) (to which our souls are fastened, but no body of any kind), and others within the cosmos (enkosmioi) (to which only bodies are fastened). And of the within the cosmos, some are heavenly 15 (ouranioi), others aetherial or fiery, others airy, others watery, others earthly, and others under Tartarus (hupotartarioi), as the poet also says,
And they call those under Tartarus...
20,1 And of the earthly ones, some rule the regions of the globe (klimatarkhai), while others maintain the cities (polioukhoi), and others belong to the house (katoikidioi).
Our allotted daimon
But we should ask which of the aforementioned six types of essential daimons they say is allotted to each person.

Well then, they say that those who live according to their own essence (kat’ 5 ousian) – that is, as they were born to live (pephukasi) – have the divine daimon allotted to them, and for this reason we can see that these people are held in high esteem in whatever walk of life they pursue (epitêdeuein). Now ‘according to essence’ is to choose the life that befits the chain from which one is suspended: for example, the military life, if from the of Ares; or the life of words and ideas (logikos), if from that of Hermes; or the healing or prophetic life, if from that of Apollo; or quite simply, 10 as was said earlier, to live just as one was born to live.

But if someone sets before himself a life that is not according to his essence, but some other life that differs from this, and focuses in his undertakings on someone else’s work – they say that the intellective (noêros) is allotted to this person, and for this reason, because he is doing someone else’s work, he fails to hit the mark in some .
But so much about the allotted daimon of each person.
The allotted daimon of Socrates
21,1 Concerning the allotted daimon of Socrates, say that three points are important to pick out (exairetos).

First, that it always used to turn him aside , and that whenever it did not turn him aside, this was a sign of encouragement. That is, since Socrates was beneficent and always eager to help everyone, like a spirited horse eager for the race, he needed the bit rather than the whip.

Second, that his allotted daimon was divine, and he makes this clear: for he says in the present dialogue that ‘My guardian is better and wiser than yours’ , and when the young man asks, ‘Who is that?’ he replies, ‘A god, Alcibiades, a god.’

Third, that he seemed to hear the voice , not because 10 was actually talking, but a kind of emanation (ellampsis) of was present in the region of his acoustic organs, and he took this to be a voice. In the same way we observe even now in common usage (sunêtheia) that those who live the priestly life, when they suddenly catch the scent of a sweet fragrance, will say (since in their case too an emanation is present in the region of the olfactory organs) that it is ‘the presence of an angel’.
Our allotted daimon in contemporary religious practice

15 But since we have discussed our allotted daimons, it is necessary to recognise that these matters are also recognised in common usage (koinê sunêtheia), albeit not by the same names. For instead of the ‘daimon’ they speak of the ‘angel’ of each of us; thus you can hear them refer to ‘your angel’ when they address those who lead the life most pleasing to god. In fact, Plato would 22,1 have made use of a word like ‘angel’, except that he left this expanse (platos) , from the heavenly to the sublunar, undivided and didn’t divide it up as the Chaldaeans do. For they divided into three, angels, daimons, and heroes; and they said that the close to the greater contained angels, the one close to us heroes, and the one in the middle daimons, the intermediaries being in the middle.

Moreover, calls Love (Erôs) a ‘god’ at one point in the Symposium, but elsewhere ‘a great daimon’. And the reason why he says ‘god’ is clear; but he addresses him as ‘daimon’ because he is an intermediary, as Love is intermediate between essence (ousia) and activity (energeia), between the beloved and the lover; and as ‘great’, since he acts beyond sensation 10 (aisthêsis), intellectively (noerôs). And for this reason Orpheus, too, says,
shepherding our thinking, eyeless and fleet, Love,
for Love is eyeless, in that he sees and hears by mind (nôi), if you consider the saying that
mind sees and mind hears.

That, then, is what the commentators say concerning daimons and their allotments; but we, for our part, will attempt to run through all this in a manner that leads to reconciliation (sumbibastikôs) with the that are current. (After all, Socrates was condemned to the hemlock for introducing new daimonic (daimonia) to the youth, and believing in gods that the state (polis) did not consider gods.)

So it should be noted that the ‘allotted daimon’ is really the ‘conscience’ (to suneidos); this is the ‘crowning peak’ of the soul, that which is faultless (anhamartêtos) in us, an unswerving judge and witness before Minos and Rhadamanthys to what here . This even becomes 5 the cause of our salvation, because it always remains faultless, and is not condemned alongside the soul for the latter’s faults, but even ‘recoils’ because of them and ‘reverts’ back to the right. And just as a child weeps in the wake of a dream because of some phantasm (phantasia) , even so does the conscience lead the soul back upward in the wake of its errors 10 (plêmmelêmata), as when says ,
What ails you? What sickness is wasting you?
and replies,
My conscience (sunesis), as I know I have done terrible things.
And from the opposite perspective, the lyric poet says,
, hope is a nurse and a good nourisher in old age.

15 Thus you would not go wrong (hamartois) by naming the allotted daimon ‘conscience’. (But it should be recognised that the of ‘consciousness’ (suneidos) concerned with our cognitive faculties (gnôstikai dunameis) is called <‘attention’, but the concerned with our faculties of desire (orektikai dunameis) is called> ‘conscience’ (suneidos), equivocally with the genus).
Son of Clinias. This can be interpreted in three ways. (1) Either the patronymic (hê ek patros klêsis) is used as an archaism, as the Poet :
20 calling each man by his father’s name and his lineage, doing honour to all,

or else, (2) since the young man cares for his reputation (philotimos) and takes 24,1 pride on account of his father (who demonstrated his excellence at the battle of Coronea and died there), he wanted to be named from him (enteuthen) because of the praise associated with that; or else, (3) it is because a patronymic is lively (diegêgermenos) and appropriate to lovers – because they are the way 5 they are and have a lot of manliness (after all, love (erôs) is either so named from strength (rhôsis) and being strong itself, or from heroism (to hêrôikon)).
Accordingly, by addressing by his patronymic, all but exclaimed
do not shame the generation of your fathers,

turning him from this toward knowledge of himself, what sort of 10 person he is and from what , and urging him towards what is noble (kalos). I think that you... This seems unworthy of Socrates’ knowledge, since it makes Socrates appear ambivalent and limited to guesswork about his proposed subject from the very start. So what can we say about this? That it indicates ignorance? Not at all, but instead the highest knowledge, to approach personalities (prosôpois) using a method that is appropriate . In this 15 case, since every young man (neos) cares about controversy and reputation – not least when it comes to standing up to strong claims – Socrates approaches Alcibiades cautiously, much as bird-catchers approach birds in a roundabout way (meth’ hupostolês) in order to avoid scaring off their quarry. Similarly, when Socrates characteristically begins the conversation in an open-ended way (dia tou distaktikou), he is aiming for the young man to be persuaded by 20 himself, and not to with a contentious attitude (enantioumenos). Are wondering... The phrase is suitable to the target (skopos) , as wonder is ‘the beginning of philosophy’. For once we wonder ‘ that it is’, we move on to ‘ why it is (dioti)’: and this is philosophy, 25,1 to express the causes (aitiai) of things – assuming that philosophy is the knowledge of beings (onta) insofar as they exist. And in another way too – for Iris is philosophy since she speaks about beings, and the poets tell the tale that she is the daughter of Wonder. And Iris herself 5 causes wonder when she appears in the air; wonder at how a mathematical shape, the circle, emerges in such material . And a certain shape is also called ‘wonder’ (thauma) among the geometers who work on linear . Why I, who was the first person to become your lover... He uses the words ‘one’ (heis) and ‘first’ (prôtos) and ‘only’ (monos) of himself, but ‘multitude’ (polloi) and ‘last’ (teleutaioi) and ‘mob’ (okhlos) of the others. 10 And we should understand that the ‘people’ (dêmos) rank before the ‘mob’, and the ‘chorus’ (khoros) before the ‘people’. For the ‘people’ are better organised (eutaktoteros) than the ‘mob’ (which is also why Paeanieus, to slander the people , says, ‘if the people are a mob, it’s the most unstable thing of all’, etc., using the word ‘mob’ for the people). But 15 the chorus is better organised than the people, since it has much unity (henôsis) and attends only to one chorus-teacher. So too Socrates, as a single individual, is on the side of good order, but he refers to the others as ‘mobbing’ (di’ okhlou).

Moreover, it was appropriate for him to comment that ‘wondered’ that his first lover had not yet abandoned him, even after a long time. For the majority of people (hoi polloi) do not judge by referring to his condition (hexis), but by referring to the 20 time . For instance, they actually suppose that those who have spent the most time in school are wise, rather than those who have spent less time, even if the latter are really wiser. Thus means that ‘you find yourself in a state of wonder when you reckon up the time that has passed since I first fell in love with you, and it’s clear that like one of the majority’. But I never even spoke to you in so many years: It is an Attic figure (skhêma) to say ‘in so many years’ (tosoutôn etôn). This means that ‘I said nothing for such a long time’. And the cause of this isn’t human: Of what? Clearly, of loving without presence. For it is not the cause of love unqualifiedly (haplôs), but of 5 godlike love, because comments that the cause of the lover’s failure to speak to (i.e. godlike love) is something daimonic and not human. And he is right to say so; for the cause of a godlike effect also has to be divine. Whose power you too will later learn: of the daimonic . This statement is meant to help the listener: because knows that is after power, he causes to 10 expect that he will discuss matters dear to his own heart (oikeios autôi), namely, what he wants.

In the phrase ‘too... later’, the word ‘too’ (kai) is superfluous. That is, it isn’t part of the syntax (sumplektikos) here, but it functions as an expletive; for did not ‘both’ (kai) learn about his power before this, so that he could ‘also’ (kai) learn about it later. The poet also uses it in this way, in the ,
15 Eurytus, to whom Apollo himself gave too a bow ,
For the ‘too’ is there not because had also handed over some other thing ; it’s just an expletive.

Also, ’ use of the word ‘later’ is explained by his remark, a little later on , that ‘When you were younger, for sure, and you were not yet full of such high hopes, I think the god prevented me from conversing with 20 you, so that I would not converse in vain – but now he has put me on the job, because now you may be ready to hear me’. But now, since it doesn’t oppose me: We should investigate why the daimonic power does not also oppose his approach to Alcibiades now, considering that is going to commit mistakes after this. For he deserted and then advised the Lacedaemonians to fortify Deceleia in his homeland, and before this he personally urged Pericles to wage the war through the writing of the decree against Megarians, in order to avoid rendering an account of the 27,1 funds spent for the Athena by Pheidias – for this was his responsibility. And another point: he caused the Mysteries to be mimed in the house of Polytion.

We offer the following reply : just as the sun does not shine selectively, but shines even upon those who do not see it – even if, on account of their own unfitness, they fail to enjoy its rays – so too the daimonic power 5 did not prevent Socrates from conversing with Alcibiades, even if he was unfit. (But against this , I think, is the fact that the daimonic power continued its opposition until the present moment: for why did it not allow him to converse at the very start?)
Xenophon’s solution is rhetorical, and here it is: that Alcibiades would have been worse than he , if he did not spend time with Socrates.

10 But the third solution is actually truer, that even if the of Socrates were not going to benefit him in this life, then nevertheless in another life (en heterôi biôi) he would recollect these and be benefited, recognising as true what was said before, and almost saying aloud,
I did not let him persuade me, and that would have been far better –

15 The same applies when, even in one and the same life, we observe certain people thinking along these lines once their passions have subsided, and only giving in to them while they are in a rage. So I have come to you: In fact, was present the whole time; so how can he say that ‘now I have come to you, since the daimonic power did not oppose it’? Well, we reply that ‘I have come’ evidently refers to his perceptible and not, as before, his solely godlike , which also lacked any presence. And I have good hopes that in the future: This also belongs to love (erôtikos), to regard benefiting the young man as a case of ‘good hope’ (euelpistia) on his behalf. And the ‘good’ is used here on account of Socrates, while 28,1 ‘hope’ on account of Alcibiades. For hope is unstable, as Herodotus also remarks, and is the ‘waking man’s dream’. It will not oppose: This is a fair statement; for if experienced no opposition before heard the words from his conscientious (sôphrôn) lips, it is clear that he will experience no opposition after Alcibiades has heard him out.
Lecture 4
With the god’s favour
Soc. Now I have been making a study of you all this time, and have just about come to understand (katanenoêka) .

Socrates is making two points here, one of which is human, the other divine. Naturally it is human to be in love, since this is common to all human beings: but it is divine to love without being present (aparousiastôs erân). He presents the cause of the second first, when he says that it is a god or a daimon. (In doing this he adopted the ancient of ‘making the end of the last into the beginning of the next’ . So Homer also says:
, Isander and Hippolochus and Laodameia: with Laodameia lay Zeus of the counsels...)

15 But now he will return to the first and express the cause of this – I mean, of love. For he loves because he looks down on the others, and he looks down on them for four reasons: because of the beauty of body, because of his good birth, because of his many friends, and because he is proud of having Pericles as guardian. For that he was beautiful in body is clear from the saying that he was ‘beloved in common of all Hellas’; from the that the Herms were 20 sculpted at Athens according to his image and likeness; and from the comment of the Cynic Antisthenes about him, ‘if Achilles was not like this, he was not in his bloom’ – about whom the Poet says, when he wants to praise Nireus for his beauty:
Nireus, the most beautiful man who came beneath Ilion, 25 Beyond the rest of the Danaans next after perfect Achilles.

29,1 And he was proud on account of his lineage, since on his father’s side he was descended from Ajax, and on his mother’s side from Alcmaeon, which was regarded as the greatest and foremost lineage in Athens and all Hellas. And he was proud on account of his friends, because – since he was ‘beloved in common of all Hellas’ (as the saying goes) – he acquired plenty of friends as a consequence. And it was certainly with justice 5 that he revered Pericles as well, considering that he was his guardian, and that he held the greatest power in his country – about whom the historian (sungrapheus) says: ‘ came to be a democracy in name, but in fact a rule by the first man’. And the comic says about him that
10 He beat the orators by sixteen paces in speaking.
It is thanks to these , then, that says that Alcibiades looked down on the others.

But if we consider that praising the youth gives him a cause for pride (huperopsia) (since this makes him even more headstrong), and praising someone to his face is the mark of a flatterer (for certain people flatter others by praising them to their face), and praising a beloved, again, makes him 15 proud – , why does Socrates praise Alcibiades on these grounds, despite the fact that he is a young man, and face-to-face, and his beloved?

Well, we reply that what appear to be words of praise now, as they are uttered by Socrates, are in reality remonstrations and refutations (elenkhoi). It was necessary for , after all, before he offered refutations that were unmixed and plain, to offer some that were mixed, in order to 20 avoid arousing and frightening off his quarry; instead, he had to approach his 30,1 quarry noiselessly, as competent bird-catchers do. Moreover, that kind of would diverge from the Socratic character (êthos); for, as we have often remarked, Socratic encouragements are like purifications drenched in honey and are unlike the of others, for instance, doctors’ incisions and burnings.

Again, when tallies up natural kinds of excellence (phusikai 5 aretai) in the course of his praises , these too are objects of both praise and criticism: criticism, on the one hand, because they arise from nature and not from discipline (askêsis) (which is why they are frequently available even to slaves, so that Plato called these kinds of excellence ‘slavish’); but praiseworthy insofar as even are named ‘excellences’ (aretai), since all excellence 10 is praiseworthy. It is clear from this, too, that refutations are offered mixed with praise.
For again, remarks at the beginning of his praises, ‘as you say’ , and by this he means, ‘as you say and not I ’, just as the Tragedian :
You hear this from yourself, and not from me.

31,1 And next, that ‘you also say that you need nothing from anybody’: for through these , he hints at Alcibiades’ rashness, since this lies beyond the weak reach of human beings, and especially of Alcibiades, who is fond of his reputation and always keeping an eye on everyone . For only a god needs nothing.

5 And third, that he says: ‘you think your resources are great and you are proud of these’, by which he means, ‘your reverence isn’t of yourself, but what lies outside of you, since you have left yourself “out of the reckoning (logos)”, as the Megarian goes’.

And fourth, that ‘your pride starts with bodily goods and ends with the of the soul, which was a mistake. For you suppose’, he means to say, ‘that you are incomparably beautiful, but it was unfitting to revere yourself for 10 your beauty, which will pass with the season (opôrâi)’. For Plato also writes in the Epigram of Laïs:
her mirror to the Paphian – for she was unwilling to behold herself as she was, but she was unable to behold herself as she used to be.
Here, he shows that one should not be proud on beauty’s account alone.

15 Again, comments that ‘You are also proud on account of your good birth’, as if to say, ‘If we adopt your standards for self-reverence, it’s possible that your ancestor was a slave twenty-five generations back.’ Another refutation comes when he remarks that ‘You think your friends are your servants’: for if, as the Pythagoreans have it, ‘friendships are equalities’, and according to Aristotle ‘a friend is another self’, why should be our ‘servants’ any more than we ourselves are? And ‘you are mistaken to be proud of Pericles as a guardian’, since this man had been shown in the Gorgias not to be a statesman (politikos). For he made his citizens neither noble nor good, but on the contrary, he made them worse: for he made them arrogant when they were angry, by providing them with dockyards, harbours, and allies; 5 consider, too, that the comic poet praises Aristides alone , since nobody good came after him.

But since every false belief takes its start from a true one (for the false, as a ‘falling away’ from the true, draws substance from it (parhuphistatai autôi) and depends upon it, lacking the power to exist in its own right: for the true, 10 through its abundance of power, influences even its contrary the false, and there is no such thing as a total darkening (amaurôsis) of the common concepts) – we need to articulate Alcibiades’ grounds for thinking that what appeared good was the greatest good, and then becoming proud about it.

We say, then, that when he was boasting about beauty, he had intelligible beauty in his mind, and he held onto an image (phantasia) of it, but since he lacked the power to obtain it truly, he started ‘fighting over shadows’, over the perceived and apparent – as the poetic verse has it,
And all about this image (eidôlon) brilliant Achaians and Trojans hewed at each other, and at the ox-hide shields strong circled guarding men’s chests...

20 Again, he revered himself for his good birth, since also in the All (to pan), what emanates from ‘better-born’ causes is treated as more deserving of honour, and superior. Thus Plato, too, comments that what derives from an unmoved cause is eternal and imperishable.

Likewise, on account of his friends, because 33,1 the origin (arkhê) of all things, which is one and single (mia kai hen), is also a unity: and friendship is like this, since, as a process of unification (henôsis), it is directed toward the One (to hen). And for his guardian (epitropos) Pericles, since he had in mind the concept (ennoia) of his allotted – for that is our true ‘guardian’ (epitropeuei).

And finally (teleutaion), Socrates says that ‘you are wealthy, too, Alcibiades, 5 but because you despise money and care about your reputation, you don’t think it’s worthwhile to be proud over your wealth’. Indeed, it is clear that despises , for the story goes that once, when the Athenians were summoned to the Assembly concerning their revenue, he voluntarily handed over ten talents from home.

Now caring for one’s reputation (to philotimon) is superior to caring for money and caring for pleasure, because spirited emotion (thumos), from which 10 the love of honour derives, has a purpose which is separable . For it provides a motivation (orexis) that resists grief, and a drive (ephesis) to defend against anyone who previously wronged . But the purpose of appetite (epithumia) – which is the source of our care for money and pleasure – is not separable, but it has been smothered by the body, either by filling up whatever it’s missing, like food and drink and other such things imported from outside, or else by letting out whatever is overflowing, like semen 15 in sexual . There are also other ways in which spirited emotion is more honourable than appetite: for when reason (logos) and appetite (epithumia) engage in battle, spirited emotion becomes the ally of reason, and, like a noble and well-born soldier, it takes up arms against appetite on reason’s behalf.

So I have just about come to understand: The text of the passage 20 supports (sumphônos) our comments. For Socrates is present, and through these words he expresses the cause of the first – I mean, of of love: and so ‘just about’ was said on Alcibiades’ account, but ‘understand’ is said on Socrates’ own account. For if we do not interpret it along these lines, then the force of his words ‘just about’ and ‘understand’ will be reversed: for this does not fit knowledge (epistêmonikos), but the 34,1 ‘just about’ does suit Alcibiades, since he is young. (Alternatively, it might make for more effective persuasion, considering character (êthikôs), like the phrase ‘I think’ above.) How you handle your lovers: Here it is clearly to understand (noein) the second cause , since Socrates says that he loves Alcibiades on account of the latter’s scornful treatment of his other 5 lovers. Even though quite a few great-minded men sprouted up: We need to investigate why he calls the crude lovers ‘great-minded’ (megalophronas). Well, we reply that the is just what we said the other day (prôên) about Love (Erôs), namely, that he influences even his contrary through an abundance of power, with the result that both are 10 called ‘lovers’ by a common name; likewise, here too we say that greatmindedness (megalophrosunê) has also provided a share of itself to its opposite, with the result that even the crude lovers are called ‘great-minded’.

It is also worth noting that has used appropriate language to address the young man in each case. Since he knows that is practically bursting to enter public life (ta koina) and rushing after a military command (stratêgikos), he describes him using words that reflect by which the young man hopes to achieve the positions that he seeks. For here he says ‘great-minded’, then ‘overwhelmed by your spirit’, and again ‘have fled’, and each and every one of these suits the statesman (politikos). I’d like to explain the reason (logos) why you felt yourself so superior: Socrates uses these words to acclimatise the young man to a life lived with 20 purpose (kat’ aitian). Consider that Alcibiades might have scorned his other lovers, not due to pride and great-mindedness, but rather due to an empty conceit (khaunotês) of the soul. But instead addresses him as someone who scorns them for a reason, not out of ignorance, but rather due to a kind of knowledge that can’t be articulated (aporrhêtê epistêmê), thus drawing him toward life lived with a cause, as we have already remarked. For when 25 says, ‘the reason why you felt yourself so superior...’, it was not entirely because of some ‘reason’ or other that looked down on them. 35,1 You say no one: These appear to be words of praise, but refutations (elenkhoi) are intermingled with them. For at the beginning he says, ‘as you say... ’. That you need no one for anything: A second refutation: for it does not belong to human power (dunamis) to need no one for anything, and especially of Alcibiades, who wants to be a statesman and a leader of people 5 (dêmagôgos), and hence needs many . For your resources: A third refutation. Beginning from the body: A fourth refutation, if at least he demonstrates through this that honours bodily goods before goods of the soul. For youthinkthat you: He means, ‘for you do not know with precision (akribôs), but you only surmise’. In the first place are the most beautiful and great: This is the first of the four indictments described in survey (theôria), on the strength of which Alcibiades proudly looked down on his lovers – namely, that he is beautiful. And it is plain to everyone to see, that you do not lie: Here he secretly refutes 15 Alcibiades, and does not praise him (which is what he appears to do). For just as the good in the god cannot be articulated in words, likewise the good in us participates in something beyond articulation. And if now he says, concerning present to Alcibiades, that it is ‘clear to everyone to see’, it is plain that this is a base thing and not truly ‘good’, so that even in these there is a refutation. 20 And next, you belong to the most vigorous lineage: This is the second on the strength of which Alcibiades proudly looks down on his other lovers. And we have pointed out that there is a refutation here as well: after all, what if his ancestor twenty-five generations back was a slave? 5 who, if anythingwereneeded, would come to your aid: Here again is another refutation: for we will come to the aid of our friends no less than they will come to ours, at least if ‘friendships are equalities’, according to the Pythagoreans, and ‘a friend is another self’, according to Aristotle. And you count on a power greater than all I have mentioned: Note that here 10 too, following everything that has been said, he has offered a speech that is appropriate (oikeios) to the young man, since he says ‘you count on a power...’: that befits a military commander’s work, and the young man is rushing to become one of these. And we have often pointed out that Socrates tries to guide his conversations in the necessary direction by using that are similar (tôn homoiôn) . So he is all but shouting aloud, ‘Learn what is true power: knowledge (epistêmê)!’ (For as he says in the Theaetetus, ‘there is nothing more powerful than knowledge existing in soul’; for this alone, and the good life, can’t be seized by tyrants nor taken away.) And I will also add the advantage of your wealth: Socrates offers this second reason for his love of Alcibiades, after the first, which was divided into four. 20 This is that Alcibiades is also ‘great’ in regard to his wealth, and actually greater than many wealthy people are. And he takes this up right away in the next , commenting, ‘and you seem to be proud of this least of 37,1 all’. For he means that ‘you aren’t proud at all of your wealth, since that you don’t revere yourself over this, because you don’t care about money (philokhrêmatos)’. You have conquered your lovers: In these too, Socrates again entices 5 the young man with the appropriateness of his language, in order to elevate him. For he says ‘you have conquered’ and again, ‘being no match for you, they were conquered’: and Alcibiades welcomes all of these . And these have not escaped you either: With these words, Socrates turns Alcibiades back toward himself and toward self-knowledge, acting to the advantage of the dialogue’s target (skopos). And in general, just as selfknowledge has a recurrent nature (apokatastatikos), likewise this discussion is recurrent, thanks to the present sentence and the following one: for at the beginning, said that ‘I think that you wonder’; and now he says this, that ‘it has not escaped you’.

Then Socrates’ arguments converge in the sentence, ‘ From this, I know very clearly that you are in a state of wonder ’. And it is certainly fair to wonder at how, at the beginning (prior to the demonstrative arguments) he made the phrase ‘you wonder’ less certain by adding ‘I think’, but now (after the demonstrative arguments) he said ‘I know well’, unambiguously: for he used the that was most useful in each case.
Lecture 5
With the god’s favour

20Alc. As a matter of fact, Socrates, perhaps you don’t realise that you just beat me to the punch. [I had already decided to come and ask you that very question: what in the world do you want? What do you hope to achieve when you crowd in on me, always making sure you’re present wherever I am? Yes, I really do wonder what you’re up to, and it would be a great pleasure to find out. Soc. Then you’ll listen to me with full attention... and I have in you a listener who will stay to hear me out? Look out: it would be no wonder if I found it as diffi cult to stop as it was to start. Alc. By all means... Speak, good man, and I will listen. Soc. Speak I must, then. It is diffi cult to play the lover with a man who doesn’t give in to lovers; all the same, I must dare to speak my mind. Alcibiades, if I saw that you were content with the advantages that I just mentioned... I would have set aside my love long ago; at least, that’s what I persuade myself. But now I’m going to show you your own, rather different plans. From that, you’ll realise that I’ve had you constantly in mind.

You see, as you seem to me, if one of the gods asked you, ‘Alcibiades, would you rather live with what you now possess, or would you rather die on the spot if you weren’t permitted to acquire anything greater?’ – it seems to me that you would rather die. But now I’ll tell you exactly what your real hope in life is. You think that as soon as you present yourself before the Athenian people, as indeed you expect to in a very few days, by presenting yourself you’ll show them that you deserve a greater reputation than Pericles himself, or anyone else who ever was. Having shown that, you’ll be the most influential man in the city, and if you’re the greatest here, you’ll be the greatest among the other Hellenes, and not only among the Hellenes...

And if that selfsame god were then to tell you that... you weren’t permitted to cross over into Asia... I think you’d rather not live with only that to look forward to; you want your reputation and your influence to saturate all mankind, to so speak. I don’t think you regard anybody as ever having been much to speak of, except perhaps Cyrus and Xerxes. I’m not guessing that this is your ambition – I know it well.]

38,1 Since we have finished learning from Socrates’ words of reason (logoi), come, let us examine Alcibiades’ utterances (phônai) too. Now, it is appropriate that we have attributed ‘words of reason’ to Socrates, but ‘utterances’ to Alcibiades. For ‘words of reason’ are appropriate to human beings, but ‘utterances’ to irrational (alogos) . Since, then, Socrates has more in common with reason (logoeidesteros), 5 whereas Alcibiades is less rational, let us treat their respective speeches accordingly.

We have learned two things from Socrates’ words: first, that Socrates loves Alcibiades, and second, that he loves him in a godlike manner (theoeidôs), that is, by attending him silently. And that – using an archaic style – articulated the cause of the second first, namely, that it is a daimonic or divine opposition. Then, in conclusion 10 (teleutaion), he introduced two causes of the first : one, that looks down on his other lovers (which, as says, he does for four reasons: beauty, good birth, friends, and Pericles as his guardian); and second, that he has not been captured by the affection of caring for money (philokhrêmaton pathos). For caring for money, although superior to caring for pleasure (for that – I mean caring for pleasure – is the lowest (eskhatos) affection of all), is nevertheless inferior to caring for one’s reputation. For the lover of reputation does exactly the same things that the good person (spoudaios) does, but the lover of reputation does them for reputation’s sake (dia timên), whereas the good person does them for the good – just as the empirical doctor does exactly what the scientific (logikos) doctor does, even though one acts with reason (logos), the other without reason or cause (aitia).

Since, then, in these we have learned about Socrates’ arguments, as 20 we have already remarked, let us now get into detail about the remainder, i.e. Alcibiades’ utterances. And these utterances express wonder at four of Socrates: the good timing (eukairia) of his words; his essence (ousia); his power (dunamis); his activity (energeia).
Four causes of Alcibiades’ wonder at Socrates

Now the good timing of words when he says this: ‘You just beat me to the punch’ – as if to say, ‘if you hadn’t just beaten 25 me to it, I would have asked you first why in the world you’ve been following me around for so long’. And consider: were there no need for the daimonic and 39,1 divine to lead the human (but this is what it amounts to for to encourage Socrates to approach Alcibiades and converse with him, by not dis couraging him); and if the actual were not prior to the potential (which it is in principle, <even if not in time>; and Socrates operates at the level of actuality, but Alcibiades at the level of potentiality) – if all that had not been so, then (he says) he would not have just beaten Alcibiades to the punch. So expresses wonder at good timing on these grounds.

Now, good timing (eukairia) has the potential to achieve the very greatest results. Consider that ‘opportunities (kairoi) are the souls of therapy’, and as Aristotle puts it, ‘opportunity is time as it seizes the moment of need (to deon)’, and ‘time as it seizes the right (to eu)’; and just as nature defines 10 the appropriate place (topos oikeios) for each body, so too she assigns a time to each action (praxis), which is called its ‘opportune’ moment (kairos). (On another note, an that needs fulfilment (teleiôsomenon) must maintain a suitable attitude toward the agent that fulfils it, just as if it were present, even if it is not present; and conversely, the agent of fulfilment should maintain such an attitude to that which is to be fulfilled, just as if it is present, even if it is not present. But this is a matter of attitude, not of timing, or rather, good timing).

Second, expresses wonder at essence when he says, ‘what do you want?’ : for what we want is good. Through this phrase, then, he has expressed wonder at the similarity of essence to the Good (agathoeides). For we all want good things: and if we also do things that are bad (kaka), it is not because we want them, but because they seem to us, as remarks in the Gorgias: in that dialogue, with the god’s favour (sun theôi), we will also discover (gnôsometha) the distinction of what we want from what seems . Subsequently in our passage too, he calls ‘good’.

40,1 Third, he expresses wonder at power (dunamis) when he says, ‘always making sure you’re present, wherever I am’. Now this belongs to a power that is sleepless and unwearied, which is also why Athene is called ‘Unwearying’ (Atrutônê). Hence it is an indication of the greatest degree of power to be present everywhere, always.

Fourth, he expresses wonder at his activity (energeia), when he says ‘you 5 crowd in on me’ (enokhleis): and this – I mean ‘crowding’ him like this – amounts to unhindered and unceasing activity. For the ‘you crowd’ (enokhleis), used just now, is not identical with the ‘in a mob’ (di’ okhlou), used earlier : consider that there, he described the crude lovers, those who wanted to act on him by means of touch (haptikôs), as being ‘in a mob’; but here, he uses the words ‘you crowd’, meaning ‘you obstruct me 10 (aporein)’, which derives from the metaphor of people walking in a crowd and being at a loss about how to move forward, just as if they are prisoners. For ‘obstruction (aporia) is a prison of the soul’, which is why its remedy (iasis), like the remedy of imprisonment, is called ‘release’ (epilusis). And Aristotle also comments in On Interpretation , ‘And this much is said in reply to the sophists as they crowd in (enokhlêseis)’, in other words, to ‘obstructions’; 15 and he also labelled obstruction a ‘crowding’ (okhlêsis), using the metaphor of a crowd. So ‘you crowd’ ‘you obstruct me’ (aporia). This, then, is what Alcibiades has to say.
Socrates’ reply

Next, Socrates imitates the leader of the philosophical chorus (koruphaios) – he who requires the fewest words, because he develops his first principles (arkhai) from the non-hypothetical. (For from our common concepts (koinai ennoiai), which have been agreed as a consensus, whereas the other skills (tekhnai), drawing their principles from hypotheses, demand many arguments: for instance, the medical takes its principles (arkhetai) from the hypothesis that human bodies are from the four elements; but it is the job of the first philosopher to prove that hypothesis, namely, first that are four and secondly that our bodies are from them). Hence Socrates, imitating the leader of the philosophical chorus (koruphaios), as we have said, and taking his principles from the non-hypothetical, demands little from Alcibiades, and what is nothing too costly: first, to hear what he has to say, and then to answer his questions. Next, with the young man nodding his agreement to do this, Socrates adds that ‘if you do this, it is in my ability to bring you that power which your other lovers did not have the power to ’.

Next, we should look into the third reason why he is in love with , namely, because the lover kindles Love and is lift ed up to this , in 10 order that he can keep the young man paying even closer attention to his words. Hence he explains that the elements and marks of the divinely inspired lover are the following two: namely, it is necessary for the divinely inspired lover to possess both judgement (krisis) and compassion (sumpatheia). For if he lacks either of these, he will not be like this : for if he has judgement but not compassion, he will be a knowledgeable but not a truly good (spoudaios) lover; and conversely, if he has compassion but not judgement, 15 he is only a crude lover. Thus it is necessary that both be present.

And where does state this? In the passage where he says, ‘It would be no wonder if I found it as diffi cult to stop as it was to start’ . For the ‘diffi cult to start’ indicates judgement (since he knew that Alcibiades was unprepared ), whereas the ‘diffi cult to stop’ indicates 20 compassion, and longing for more of his beloved. Aside from this (allôs), the diffi culty in starting was due to Alcibiades himself, since (as we have remarked) he was unprepared: but Socrates’ diffi culty in stopping is due to himself. For Socrates, who is always longing to help youths and to do them good, will not stop until he brings his beloved to fulfilment. So he says that ‘it was diffi cult (khalepon) even now to approach you’: and he is right to use the 42,1 word ‘diffi cult’ instead of ‘easy’ or ‘impossible’. For it was not easy, since it was not feasible for to divert Socrates in the same way as he scorns his other lovers; nor, for the same reason, was it impossible. That is, once he began 5 to scorn the other , Socrates’ approach was no longer impossible; for it had been impossible for him to hear Socrates out without looking down on the others.

Having said this, and having kindled love to this point, reveals the third reason when he adds that, ‘because I scorn your resources, I love you, and I have not abandoned you for all this time – because 10 I know you really don’t desire these appearances’.

Now it is not the case that all human beings desire the same experiences (pathê) – for example, one cares for reputation, another cares for money and riches, another cares for pleasure. And the pleasure-lover longs for divine ease, about which it has been said, ‘the gods who live at ease’ – that is the kind of idea that this person has in mind, but since he is unable to attain it, he fights over shadows (skiamakhein), the reflections and expressions of this . And the money-lover longs for fulfilment and self-suffi ciency, because self-suffi ciency and fulfilment are divine – and so he desires this; but since he is unable to attain , he grasps after it by loving money. And again, the reputation-lover longs for the god who is suffi cient and freely giving, even if he is unable to attain this. (But being fulfilled (teleion) and being suffi cient (hikanon) are not identical; for fulfilment is just needing nothing 43,1 from another, whereas suffi ciency is a matter not only of having no needs, but also being able to give freely to others. And the reputation-lover wants to appear to be such a person). And since Alcibiades thinks little of his own 5 resources, this is the approach that Socrates deploys. For he introduces the god when he asks him ‘whether you prefer, Alcibiades, to let the life of great works fall by the wayside and to be content with what you have, or to die?’, and then, offering an answer himself on Alcibiades’ behalf, ‘prefer to die’.

After this, he divides up Alcibiades’ entire life, and says that ‘you hope to 10 approach the people in a few days and to advise the Athenians’. Now this was at the stage just preceding adolescence (ephêbias); in ten days, as Proclus relates, was to be enrolled among the Ephebes (ephêboi), and it was the custom that no one could give advice to the Athenians before being enrolled among them. ‘And so,’ continues, ‘you are about to offer advice, and you suppose that on this basis you will get a reputation, and then 15 be honoured in the city, and not only here, but also in Attica and Hellas, then among the Hellenes and throughout all Europe – and not here alone, but even in Asia and through the whole earth: and you will count no other person as worthy of notice and wonder beyond yourself, save Cyrus and Xerxes.’ So says Socrates.
The god questions Alcibiades: 105A–C

20 But come, let us look into the god’s questions, and the philosopher’s answers to the god on behalf of Alcibiades, what lessons (dogmata) we should take away from the god’s questions and the philosopher’s answers. And first of all, let us articulate the reason why made a god question Alcibiades, and then made himself answer on behalf.

Well, then, he made a god pose the questions for three reasons: first, in order that the young man might not deny his own words, since we have all learned to trust that the divine is aware of even our chance movements, if indeed it is true that
All things are full of god, and he hears all things, right through rocks and 44,1 through the earth and within a man himself, who has concealed his thought (noêma) in his breast.

The second explanation would be that Socrates staged this scene because of his fondness for tragedy. Certainly is keen on this kind of thing: hence, just as the often produce a ‘god from the machine’ (mêkhanê) to resolve disasters (as in the Alcestis of Euripides, the playwright put Apollo in the house of Admetus), so Socrates similarly introduced a god in this case. According to a third explanation, it is because Socrates, who is a lover, wants to bring himself into union with his beloved, both as a consequence of his compassion , and because the divine is a unity (henas) beyond being; meanwhile, he wants to 10 fulfil his beloved according to his judgement (krisis), and the divine also acts for fulfilment (teleiôtikos). And he made himself answer for Alcibiades, since the interval (meson) between god and Alcibiades was wide, and it would have been empty (kenon), had Socrates not placed himself in this position.

But let us look at the remainder , what lessons (dogmata) 15 emerge from the god’s questions. (For the questions and answers themselves have already been stated). From the questions, then, it emerges that lives (bioi) 45,1 by choice (kath’ hairesin) and not by the compulsion of necessity: for he says, ‘What do you want?’ So too in the Timaeus responsibility (aitia) lies with the one who chooses, but ‘the god is blameless (anaitios)’ ; and again in Republic, ‘you will choose a daimon; a daimon will not be allotted to you’. For it is up to us (en hêmin) to choose a life of a certain kind; but it is not up to us whether we who made the choice will act out (prattein) the consequences of that life, but this is compelled by necessity – just as it is up to us (eph’ hêmin) to throw a stone, but the stone’s landing, once it is released, is not up to us. So we must express it in the poetic verse,
... Yet I am not responsible (aitios), 10 But Zeus is, and Destiny, and Fury the holy wanderer...

And the following lessons from the answers: that it is more profitable not to exist than to exist badly; for he says, ‘You, I think, would choose to die rather than live like this.’ Second, that the body is an impediment to obtaining excellence (aretê), from the same – for if he prefers to die, it is clear that he chooses this because the body is an 15 impediment to what he desires (epithumei). And the third lesson is that you should not give advice (sumbouleuein) to your advisees with a view to your own reputation (timê), but instead, with a view to benefiting those who listen to you. Alcibiades, on the other hand, wants to approach the people with reputation in view (dia timên). Fourth, that you should judge the reputation-lover by the quality of the people who honour him, and not by those who happen to find him worthy of wonder – just as Alcibiades wants to be an object of wonder to Hellenes and barbarians and all human beings. Fift h, that the examples (paradeigmata) which he introduced were dissimilar (anomoia) , namely, Cyrus and Xerxes: for Cyrus was called ‘father’ on account of his gentle character and tolerance toward his subjects, whereas Xerxes ‘despot’ on account of his extreme irascibility and use of overpowering force (for this man was aroused 46,1 not only against human beings, but even against nature herself and the elements: as Aristides says, ‘he strode on the sea by yoking the Hellespont, and he sailed the land by cutting Athos, and he hid the sun when he gave the order to fire’); and Darius was a mean between these, who was called ‘the dealer’ on account of his love of money. For he ordained the tribute for the Persians, as Herodotus says, and he was the one who secured his own throne by a horse’s whinny, since it was the Persian custom for children to succeed to kingships.

That is the content of the survey (theôria). 10 As a matter of fact, Socrates, perhaps you don’t realise that you just beat me to the punch... See how the text agrees with what was said in the survey (theôria). In these words, you see, Alcibiades expresses wonder at Socrates’ good timing – which has the greatest power (dunatai) in all things, as has been demonstrated. For Socrates would not have just beat him to the punch, were it not for the reasons we have explained. 15 What in the world do you want? Here he expresses wonder at the essence of , which is good: for what we want is good. And we have commented that what is wanted is not the same as what appears to be , as had been explained in the Gorgias . What do you hope to achieve when you crowd in on me? He made activity (energeia) clear in the phrase, ‘you crowd’. But the phrase ‘you crowd’ (enokhleis) used just now, and the phrase ‘in a mob’ (di’ okhlou) used earlier do not come to the same thing, as we have learned. And next he expresses wonder at power (dunamis). Always making so sure you’re present, wherever I am. See how he has also conveyed power here. For it belongs to a power that is sleepless and unwearied to be present and accompanying everywhere. 25 And it would be a great pleasure to find out. It has also been explained in the survey that even the pleasure-lover does not long for this apparent pleasure, but rather for true ; not, however, being able to obtain it, he fights over a shadow, namely, its appearance. And the phrase ‘a great pleasure’ has provided us with the opportunity to make this observation (epistasis): for the passage is appropriate to the pleasure-lover. 5 Then you’ll listen to me... Here Socrates imitates the leader of the philosophical chorus and asks for little, in keeping with the philosophy that does not rely on hypotheses. And he says here that ‘it is in my ability to bring you that power which your other lovers did not have the power to ’, in order that will listen to his words now, and answer him a little later on. 10 And I have in you a listener who will stay to hear me out? This was intended as a question, and it ought to be read this way . The reply to him makes this clear: for adds ‘by all means’ after has asked the question. Look out: it would be no wonder if I found it as diffi cult to stop as it was to start. Here we should articulate the third reason , 15 but he has not done so, in order that he might kindle his love for the young man even more; nonetheless, he does explain the elementary features of the divine lover. He does not do so plainly, but they are from what follows on his words: for he says, ‘just as diffi cult as it was for me to begin’, and reveals from this his quality of judgement (krisis) – for it stems from judgement not to begin at random, or by chance. And then he adds, ‘it may be just as 20 diffi cult for me to stop’, and this clearly displays his compassion (sumpatheia), since when remains close to his beloved for a long time, that stems from compassion.

In fact, this is just what the divine is like: it begins gradually and stops gradually, furnishing abundant goods for human beings to the recipients’ suitability (epitêdeiotês). For we see that those who are successful (eutukhountas) struggle to succeed at first, but remain successful for a long 25 time; the same goes for those who are unfortunate (dustukhountôn) and those who receive corrective treatment (kolazomenôn). It should be recognised, you see, that the divine is really always productive of goods, and does not act intermittently, but is a constant fount of such . Also, the goods that 48,1 derive from it are divided, since some are primary, others secondary. Goods produced in the primary sense, then, are those that the genuinely successful possess – I mean in children, words, wealth, and basically everything like this; and secondary goods are those that corrections (kolaseis) of errors (hamartêmatôn).
