Yes, these are also good things, for we should not countenance the idea that the divine would ever do a bad deed: those who shrink from their sentences resemble children trying to escape medical incisions. Thus the divine is constantly providing goods, and the recipients, based on their suitability, have the benefit of either the primary goods or the secondary; and these both begin and stop gradually. 10 Speak, good man, and I will listen. Also notice how in the text he calls ‘good’: he has expressed wonder at his essence as similar to the Good (agathoeidês) not only by ‘you want’. It is diffi cult to play the lover with a man who doesn’t give in... We have already observed that he neither used ‘impossible’ nor ‘easy’, and we have recognised that he was right to do this. All the same, I must dare... He speaks well when he calls the procession to the secondary ‘daring’ (tolman): the Pythagoreans likewise called the Dyad ‘daring’, as first having dared to separate itself from the Monad. It is also necessary that the soul, descending into genesis, which is a labyrinth (laburinthos), should make use of the monad as a thread for its 20 wandering here , just as Theseus the thread of Ariadne for the Cretan labyrinth. For if I, Alcibiades, : Here is the third reason why Socrates is in love: for he says that he thinks little of resources and does not really prize (agapan) the four that he listed off a little earlier . This will be shown, you see, from the god’s subsequent 25 questions and answers to them. I would have set aside long ago: Harpocration got involved at this point; by paying close attention to the language, he proved that the words require Socrates to be a divinely inspired lover. It is clear that he is a divinely inspired lover because he says here, ‘I would have put aside long ago’, but the crude lover does not set aside whenever he wishes, because he is experiencing this state due to an affection (pathos): and we do not set aside our affections whenever we wish, any more 5 than we begin experiencing them . Now this man begins when he wishes, and he wishes when his beloved is worthy of love. So he also stops when he wishes, just as here, too, he remarks that ‘had I observed you really going after apparent goods, I would have set aside my love long ago’. 10 But now I’m going to show you your own, rather different plans: He means, ‘Since you do not truly desire these things, but other, greater things, and you fight over shadows because you are ignorant about the latter, I will tell you the arguments by means of which I will prove that you do not really long for these things.’ And he added the ‘you your own’, demonstrating that he knows what belongs to better than he does himself. That’s also 15 why he added, ‘From that, you’ll realise that I’ve had you constantly in mind’ – meaning, ‘ from my telling you the truth about yourself’. And the ‘I have spent all this time thinking about you’ also has to do with love. You see, as you seem to me, if one of the gods asked you... Here begin the 20 questions of the god. The reason why he introduced a god to question Alcibiades has been stated in the survey. Would you rather live with what you now possess: From this one can derive the doctrine, which we have also stated, that lives are according to choice, and not according to necessity. And this is clear in the Republic as well. 25 It seems to me that you would rather die: This is the answer given by the philosopher on the young man’s behalf: and we should notice that, although he is just one actor ‘on stage’ (en heni prosôpôi), he preserves the form of dialogue 50,1 here, himself introducing the questions as if they came from a god, and the answers as if they came from Alcibiades. And there are two lessons to be drawn from the speech: that it is better not to exist than to exist badly, and that the body is an impediment to the acquisition of excellence. 5 But nowI’ll tell you just what your real hope in life is: From this point begins the division of Alcibiades’ life: for Socrates unfolds his entire chain of reasoning in the following words. as indeed you expect to in just a few days... Proclus relates that after twenty days was to be enrolled among the Adolescents (ephêboi), and then was to advise the Athenians. That you deserve a greater reputation than Pericles himself: Another lesson emerges from this point: one should not give advice for the sake of reputation, as Alcibiades does now, but for the benefit of one’s hearers. And we should recognise that , by saying ‘greater than Pericles himself’, begins from the source (hestia) of ambition, and what is dearest to his heart (oikeios). 15 And if you’re the greatest here, you’ll be the greatest among the other Hellenes, and not only among the Hellenes: has his speech (logos) proceed like a ladder: for he adds, ‘you want to be famous (eudokimein) not only among the Hellenes, but all through Europe too, among foreigners, and across the whole totality of the Earth’, and ‘you think no one worth speaking of, except Cyrus and Xerxes’.
20 And I say that will not stop caring about his reputation even when he reaches this point, but he will want even more – as the comic poet puts it:
even if he achieves this, he wants forty times as much.

For as we remarked before, it is not the case that all human beings long for just the same affections (for these are unlimited), but they long for more, because they possess a concept (ennoia) of certain other things that they are unable to secure.

25 We should also investigate why the affection of caring for reputation is the most diffi cult of all to wipe out (dusekniptos). Consider: it is so 51,1 that even those who decide not to care about their reputation, do that out of care for their reputation, that is, in order not to appear to care about their reputation. We assert, then, that the affection of caring for reputation is diffi cult to wipe out for the following reason: it is closer to reason (logos) than other are, and is sibling to it, and reason is not something we can cast 5 aside; therefore what is close to reason is also diffi cult for us to cast aside.

Or here is an alternative reason: the soul, when it descends here and flees slavery to its superiors, but wants to rule over its inferiors, first clothes itself in care for reputation from among the affections; and then, when it casts aside, it discards this one last of all. Since it is also said of ,
10 Then he stripped off his rags.

And we should recognise that among our vital (zôtikais) capacities, the reputation-loving affection is diffi cult to cast aside, while among our cognitive (gnôstikais) capacities it is imagination (phantasia) that is diffi cult to cast aside. For imagination is always available to our soul, as our soul is constantly fashioning impressions (tupous) of what it does not know, and bestowing 15 shapes, sizes, and bodies on the non-bodily, and confining the god in terms of place (topôi). That selfsame (autos) god... It was fitting for him to locate ‘self’ (autos) on the level of the god, since the god is the unit (henas), and unitary in form (henoeidês). But he spoke in the plural about the realities (pragmata) that Alcibiades is questing after, because the that follow and extend from the divine and the monad are many, and every person quests for these. That 20 he spoke in the plural about these is clear also from his introducing , ‘to add something to the realities (pragmata) that are there’. And the word ‘add’ also suits Alcibiades. Except Cyrus and Xerxes: It has been pointed out that he made use of dissimilar examples: for these were not selected for the same reason, 25 considering that one was called ‘father’, the other ‘despot’. 52,1 I’m not guessing (eikazô) that this is your hope – I know it well. It was fitting that he placed the ‘I know well’ after the demonstrations (apodeixeis), as he did at the beginning too . It is like the Homeric to say, as Diomedes said to Athena, ‘Nor do I escape your notice when I move,’ but Socrates from the opposite point of view : ‘nor do you 5 escape my notice’, since he says: ‘I know well, then, and am not just guessing that you have this hope.’

10 Two had been advanced in the proem : first, why does Socrates love ? And second, why does Socrates accompany him by loving in silence (that is, why does he love him without being present with him)? In answer to the second , the cause has been attributed to a daimonic or divine entity. In answer to the first , three causes have been stated: that Alcibiades looks down on the other lovers, that he cannot be conquered by love of money, and 15 that he thinks little of his resources. Since the proem encompassed not only these two , but also a third – that Socrates does not abandon after the other lovers have ceased? – Socrates is now in position to impart the cause of this. And so he explains, ‘Here is why I do not abandon you: it is because I am the 20 only person who has the power to give you the power that all of your other lovers could not give’.
Three puzzles (aporiai) 1. Why does Socrates vaunt himself?

Now first of all, we raise the puzzle (aporoumen), why is Socrates boastful here? – he who is everywhere ironic, and about whom it is said, ‘this is your habitual irony, Socrates’; who is always claiming that he knows nothing, and teaches nothing, which is also why the god at Delphi said about him that
Socrates is wisest of all men

– since it was not only by striking the air, by vocal expression, that used to say this sort of thing, but through his 5 manner of living, and in his divine inspiration. We ought to investigate, then, how it could be that such a person thinks like this in the present case, announcing that he alone is able to deliver power to the youth.

Well, we reply, first, that the philosopher boasts at the right moment (kairos): for before this, it was crucial that he not boast, since Alcibiades scorned him just as he scorned his other lovers. So Socrates understood the right moment for 10 boasting. In fact, he has often done this: for example, in the Theaetetus, after establishing himself as a judge between ‘genuine’ and ‘wind-egg’ theories (logoi), he says, ‘For no god ever has ill-will toward a human being, nor do I do this out of any ill will, but it is never lawful (themis) for me either to agree to falsehood or to suppress truth.’ (Notice how he ranked himself with the god here, by saying, ‘For no god ever has ill-will... ’) And again in the Apology he boasts when he says, ‘It is not permissible (themis) for a better person to be ruled by a worse one’; and again in the same dialogue when he says that ‘Anytus and Meletus have the power to kill me, but not to do me any harm at all’ (in the first part of this sentence, he 20 uses the word ‘me’ in the more ordinary way, referring to the composite (sunamphoteron) ; but in the second part, he uses it in its strict sense (kuriôs), referring to the soul alone).

So that is one solution , that he knows how to be boastful at the right moment. A second solution is that he is not being boastful 54,1 (megalorrhêmonei) when he prefers himself to base people with a herd mentality (agelaioi). For it is nothing to boast about (mega) when the philosopher achieves what worthless people lacked the power to achieve.

And here is a third : for someone who pays precise attention (akribôs ennoêsêi) to the words used here, it does not seem as if Socrates is 5 boastful at all. For he says, ‘with the god’s support, of course’ , and ‘It is impossible to put any of these plans (dianoêmata) of yours into effect without me’ . (The word ‘without’ is a material (hulikos) preposition, and suitable to matter (hulê), since ‘without’ matter there is nothing here to think about).
2. Why does Socrates vaunt Alcibiades?

Second, we raise the puzzle, why does Socrates make the young man arrogant 10 by holding out such hopes and pronouncing that he will deliver power to him? Well, we say that just as the doctors do not apply themselves to the causes of a disease until they have made it less acute (for which reason it was well said by Hippocrates, ‘ medicate and attack when it is ripe, not raw nor at the beginning’), likewise Socrates does not apply himself to the affections (pathê) before he has ameliorated 15 them, nor does he extirpate them ‘by burning and incisions’, as the saying goes.

For we need to understand that – just as we said at the beginning – there are three methods (tropoi) of purification, the Pythagorean, Socratic and Peripatetic or Stoic. Now, the Stoic heals opposites by opposites, introducing appetite (epithumia) to spirited emotion (thumos), thus soft ening , and introducing spirited emotion to appetite and so strengthening , encouraging it to mature into manhood (anagôn pros to 20 andrikôteron). This is analogous to heated rods: if someone wants to straighten one, he bends it backwards, in order that symmetry might occur when it curves back in the opposite direction: in the case of souls, similarly, it was their custom 55,1 to foster harmony by using this method .

But the Pythagorean urges us to ‘concede a little’ to the affections (pathê), and to taste them as if ‘with the tip of the finger’: the doctors talk about this as ‘a little worse’ (smikrôi elatton). What they meant to convey was this: 5 those who are swelling up with an affection will be unable to stay in control of it, unless they act on it. For this is also what Athena did in the case of Pandarus: when he wanted to break his oath, she conceded to him, which is also why he received corrective punishment (kolazomenos) through his tongue, since this became the instrument of his oath-breaking.

But the Socratic method of purification converts likes to likes: by saying to 10 someone who loves possessions, ‘learn what true self-suffi ciency is’, or to someone who loves pleasure, ‘ what divine ease is’, and basically everything that we stated earlier. And this method is superior to the others: for the first heals one trouble by another, since an affection by an affection, while the second does not allow the soul to remain spotless, on account of its contact with the affections.
3. Why does Socrates claim that he can deliver power to Alcibiades?
15 Third, then, we raise the puzzle (aporoumen), why does Socrates claim that he has the power (dunasthai) to provide power (dunamis) to Alcibiades?

Well, we should reply to this as follows: he means that he will provide knowledge (epistêmê) to him, and knowledge is a kind of power, since elsewhere he remarks that ‘nothing is more powerful (dunatôteron) than demonstration existing in the soul’ (and ‘demonstration’ is of knowledge), and that knowledge is invincible to a tyrant.

20 Or that Socrates, who is an outstanding person (spoudaios), is self-suffi cient (autarkês) and is kin (sungenês) to the self-suffi ciency of the god, and therefore here, as a lover, he applies outstanding effort (spoudazei) to providing this kind of self-suffi ciency to his beloved, to completing him, and to guiding him upward toward the god’s self-suffi ciency.

Or thirdly, that, according to the boastful talk of the Stoics, only the ‘ruler’ (arkhikos) – that is, the person who knows how to rule (arkhein) – is in control (arkhôn), even if he lacks the tools to exercise the ruler’s knowledge; and only the wise man is wealthy, that is, the man who knows how to make use of the wealth that is available, even if no wealth is in fact available. This is the kind of ‘power’, then, that Socrates announces to the youth as for his statesmanhood (politikos); for it is true that alone, and none of the others, had the ability to 5 provide this. Toward the end of the proem (prooimion) , he makes the second of that we pointed out – I mean, that answer his questions. And here we ask again, why in the world does the philosopher ask Alcibiades to do this?

We reply that Socrates did not want to draw dead and unbreathing words 10 (logoi) from him, but (so to speak) active and living , suitable to people engaged in dialectic; and this is what he is hunting for in the answers.

Alternately, that Socrates, being a lover, wants to embrace (periplokê) his beloved; and the dialogue form is similar to an embrace, as the interaction through brief exchanges becomes a process of question and answer.

15 Alternately, that, as he says in the Phaedrus, ‘it is necessary for the speech (logos) to resemble a living being (zôiôn)’; and it follows that the best-constructed speech must resemble the best of living beings. And the best living being is the cosmos: just as this serves as a meadow for a diversity (poikilôn) of living beings, the speech should likewise be full of all kinds of characters (prosôpôn). And in other ways, since, just as in this all things speak and act (for the activities of beings are like their voices), so too in the speech it is appropriate for all of its characters to speak, just as it is for everyone to act (energein).

Fourth, that the form of question and answer is stimulating and tends to revert (epistreptikos). Naturally, the orators too, when they wish to stimulate the audience or turn their attention to the speech, have used this : for example, ‘answer 25 me, by the gods!’ But a speech that drones on at length makes the audience fall 57,1 asleep: as Aischines says, for instance, ‘dreaming over the pronouncement of justice’. So Socrates, who wants to revert Alcibiades , asks him to answer his questions.

That completes our survey (theôria) and the proem (prooimion) of the dialogue; here, then, commences the remainder of the first part (prôton meros), which is the refutative . ‘Well then, Socrates, what’s this got to do with your point (logos)? You said you were going to tell me why you haven’t abandoned me.’ Notice that Alcibiades himself asks Socrates to explain the third point that he mentioned in the proem, namely, why ‘when the others have stopped, he alone 10 does not abandon him’ – and, a little later, Socrates will answer this too. Yes, I will tell you, my dear son of Clinias and Dinomache. It is neither untimely nor excessive to address by his father’s and mother’s names here, as someone might have supposed. Rather, considering the young man’s noble birth on both sides, it is appropriate to use these words to express the point that ‘neither your relatives on your mother’s side, nor those 15 on your father’s side, can offer you the power that I can provide’. It is impossible to put any of these plans (dianoêmata) of yours into effect without me. ‘This’, he means, ‘is the reason why I do not abandon you, since you cannot obtain what you hope for without me.’

And he uses the word ‘plans’ (dianoêmata) about the that he described earlier, when he said that ‘you think that you will approach the 20 Athenians quite soon, and show them that you deserve a reputation even greater than Pericles himself, and you will prove your importance among Hellenes and foreigners’, and basically everything that we have discussed in that passage. And the phrase ‘without me’, as a preposition indicating materiality, shows that the philosopher is not boasting, as has been stated in the lecture (theôria). For your practical affairs (pragmata) and for you yourself... He says ‘for 25 your practical affairs’ meaning ‘for your activities (energeiai)’, and ‘for you yourself (autos)’ meaning ‘for your soul’, just as he used the word ‘me’ most strictly of the soul in the Apology when he said, ‘but they do not have the power to harm me ’. 58,1 I think this is why the god hasn’t allowed me to talk to you all this time, meaning: ‘if the god used to turn me away before in order that I did not speak in vain, then now, since he does not turn me away, I will provide you with the power that you desire by any means at my disposal’. For if the god turned him aside then (when it was appropriate to do so), it is not in vain that the god does 5 not do so now. For if the good man (spoudaios) does nothing in vain, and neither does nature (phusis), then the god must to an even greater degree. For just as you hope to demonstrate in public... Here Socrates offers an analogy: ‘for the rank that you hold in relation to the citizens, Alcibiades – surpassing them to the degree that an adviser surpasses those whom he advises 10 (for the adviser must be like this) – this is that I hold in relation to you, and the god in relation to me’. Demonstrating that I’m worth the world to you... We should notice that the philosopher always associates ‘demonstration’ (endeixamenos) with the dialogue form, but ‘display’ (epideixamenos) with extended speech; this is also the reason why he always distinguishes these from one another. So here too, he utilises this , when , ‘I will prove (deixô) to you, 15 using question and answer, the magnitude of power that will come to you through me.’ With the god’s support, of course... Notice, again, a sign that Socrates is not boasting; for he did not only say that he himself was able, but ‘with the god’. 20 When you were younger... Here he repeats what he said above. For he 59,1 was saying then, ‘I think this is also why for a long time the god has not allowed me to converse with you’: and that is also what he means now. He hinted riddlingly (êinitteto) at this remark in the beginning, as we noticed there, when he said, ‘the power of which you will also learn later’: here, then, 5 is the follow- up to that remark, namely, that ‘ prevented me so that I would not converse with you in vain’. That’s also why he added, ‘but now he sent me , for now you might listen to me’, using these words to urge even more strongly to listen to him, since the god, by not turning aside, sent him to talk with so that the latter might be persuaded. Now you seem much more strange (atopos)... , more paradoxical and more worthy of wonder. And it is appropriate that Socrates seems more wondrous to Alcibiades now, after he has conversed with him, than when he was silent. For in our case too, we wonder more at the divine when we are visibly illuminated and inspired than when we are not. Well, on the question of whether or not these are my ambitions, you already seem to have your mind made up. Since Alcibiades is naturally gift ed (euphuês), he neither denies absolutely that he has in mind what Socrates 15 stated, nor does he grant it, but he creates a middle ground (khôrei) in between by using hypothetical language (dia tou hupothetikou skhêmatos).

He does not grant , because in a democracy it was customary for the speaker not to appear keen on power, and so he shrank from this; but he does not deny it either, because he wished (since he wanted to become a politician) to hear from Socrates what kind of words such a person would need to use to be appointed to power over the people. Thus he 20 says, ‘Even supposing I do have in mind what you say, how will you provide it for me?’ How will they be achieved through you...? Here the philosopher Iamblichus got involved, and raised the puzzle (aporein) that Alcibiades appears more fulfilled (teleioteros) than Socrates. For said ‘ through you’, a 60,1 preposition that suits an instrumental cause, whereas said ‘ with the god’, a preposition suitable to a productive (poiêtikos) cause, and he put himself on the level (sunetaxen) of the god; but said ‘through you’ as if Socrates were an instrument of the god.

And solved this absolutely beautifully (pankalôs) by pointing 5 out that Plato, in his other , claims that more fulfilled souls watch over in this world (têide) jointly with the god, and jointly set them in order, but less fulfilled souls have the function of an instrument, and so the god uses them with a view to here (entautha). (In fact, does not only use less complete , but there are even times when bad , for instance, murderers with a view to the rendering of the proper, just penalty (dikê) for those who owe it). Thus Socrates, with reference 10 to his own, more fulfilled capacities (dunameis), said ‘ with the god’; but Alcibiades was referring to his less complete , and so he said ‘ through you’ and again added ‘and without you’, the preposition suitable to matter (hulê). Then are you asking if I can say some long speech, like the ones you’re used 15 to hearing? By this , Socrates aims to prepare Alcibiades not to expect long speeches from him. For he was sure that Alcibiades, who is disposed to oratory, would expect him to converse this way, which is why he says ‘such as you are accustomed to hear’. And he implants the concept (ennoia) that he will speak dialectically (dialogikôs): for he adds, ‘this sort of thing is not my , 20 but to demonstrate to you...’, meaning, ‘to converse by question and answer’. If only you were willing to do just one brief service... Here Socrates makes a different request of Alcibiades, that is, to answer. And he says ‘brief’ because he practises the philosophy that does not require hypotheses, and does not require many words. We have stated in the survey (theôria) the reasons why he asks him to answer. At this point it should also be noted that answers will make him appear to be set straight by his own, self-moved activity (autokinêtôs) – i.e. through cross-examination (elenkhos) by himself. For we 5 need to understand that we act in a self-moving way when we revert upon ourselves, needing no one else to be set straight and to achieve relief from the affections (pathê) in us; but whenever we put a stop to our affections through others ’ cross-examination, then that amounts to being moved by another (heterokinêtôs). This is also the case in the Gorgias – for there, through Socrates’ cross-examination of the spirited emotion (thumos) of Thrasymachus, we learn (ennooumen) how to put a stop to the Thrasymachus 10 in us. And likewise by Callicles’ love for pleasure and Polus’ love for reputation . So too by Protagoras’ appearance (phantasia): for Protagoras is a sophist, and appearance is quite similar to the sophist, since it misrepresents (sophizein) and remodels realities. And so Socrates, who wants Alcibiades to act with self-movement here, 15 prepares him to give answers: and he calls this ‘doing a service’, in order that the person who desires rule over all should be shown, in this case, to be Socrates’ servant. Well, as long as the service you mean is nothing onerous (khalepos): The young man gives an appropriate answer to this sort of request from Socrates, considering that will provide to him a power which the others were not able , and he supposed the request would be a large one. This is why he replies, ‘If you mean nothing onerous’: for he imagined that the request would match the magnitude of the results promised. But notice, he nevertheless agrees to do the service for Socrates, on the condition that it would not be burdensome (baru).

And answers, ‘If it seems onerous to give answers’, in order that 62,1 , agreeing that it is not onerous, will readily give answers. Of course the young man replies, ‘It is not onerous’; and this is well said. For if Aristotle were the questioner – or some other combative (eristikos) who looks just to victory and on that account delights in the speaker’s mistakes in conversation – then it would be diffi cult and onerous to give answers; but 5 since it is Socrates, the ‘midwife’ who aims to benefit youths and set them straight, it is suitable ‘not onerous’. On the contrary, it is the questioning that is onerous, just as on a journey to lead than to follow. Then I question you as someone who has this plan in mind? We must take 10 this as a question, since the answer, again, makes it plain that it is . For answers, ‘Let’s say that I do.’ We should recognise that in his present response, Alcibiades is again offering a hypothetical answer – with rhetorical brilliance, since he was manifestly well educated in by Pericles, who was also brilliant, and his guardian. Therefore he says, ‘Let’s say I do, if you like, so that I can find out what you’re going to say.’ (The phrase ‘if you 15 like’ (ei boulei), you see, is hypothetical.) As for the rest , it suits his character (êthikôs) as a person who does not resist agreement.
With that, the proem (prooimion) of the dialogue is completed, and the beginning of the refutative follows.
Here Begins the First Section
Lecture 7
With the god’s favour
20Soc. Come on, then: I say that you intend to come forward and advise the Athenians

There are three basic components of being a good adviser, as follows: good intentions (prohairesis agathê), exact knowledge (gnôsis akribês), and expressive ability (dunamis apangeltikê) (for the adviser must have goodwill for his 63,1 audience, or else he is no good ; and obviously he also needs exact understanding about the subject he is going to discuss, since he is not about to give advice out of ignorance; and moreover, he also must be able to express what he had in mind and put it into words, or else the first two are useless). Given these , then, Socrates demonstrates that Alcibiades is not a good adviser on the grounds of exact knowledge. He begins by using the following proof: 1. The good adviser understands the subject of his advice, and [understands
it] better than those whom he advises.
a. For not on an equal footing (for
it would be pointless to teach people what they already know);
b. But it is also not inferior (for it would be madness for someone who
doesn’t know something to explain it to people who do);
10 c. It follows by necessity that the good adviser understands the subject
of his advice better than his audience. 2. The person with superior understanding either learned
or discovered it.
a. Because knowledge is twofold, being divided into learning and
discovery. For we ‘learn’ when the movement comes from someone
else (heterokinêtôs), and we ‘discover’ when the movement comes
from ourselves (autokinêtôs).
i. This is also how the poets portray Hermes, who is the overseer
of knowledge, as both a messenger (angelos) and the son of
Maia: he is ‘messenger’ as a learner, because the messenger
announces things he learns from others; and he is the son of
15 Maia as a discoverer, because the midwife (maia) does not
herself place infants into the women who give birth to them, but
she brings into the light that are already there. In
the same way, then, the discoverer brings to birth the
explanations (logoi) that are within him.
ii. And if learning is sometimes superior to discovery – for
20 instance, when we learn from gods through dreams – we
should recognise that in this situation, activity motivated
by another is actually preferable to activity motivated by
oneself: for it benefits us to be led by a god rather than by
ourselves. 64,1 3. Next, the learner or discoverer either conducted an investigation or

can tell of a time when he didn’t think that he understood and so

did not understand. But obviously Alcibiades is not able to make this

age-mates, he swore that they were cheating him (hup’ autôn adikeisthai),

as if he had a precise fix on justice (to dikaion). That is how the proof proceeded synthetically. But it is also possible to 10 present it analytically, as follows: 1. The good adviser is able to state the time at which he did not think he

understood. 2. Such a person either conducted an investigation or received instruction. 3. Such a person either learned or discovered. 4. Such a person understands the subject of his advice better than those
whom he advises. 5. The good adviser, then, understands the subject of his advice better than

his audience. 15 The first proof resembles a descent of the soul that is continually assuming, or clothing itself in, affections (pathê), the second an ascent that is continually casting affections off. Hence one might also recite the poetic verse about this,
Then he stripped off his rags...

But Socrates tests Alcibiades not only by the proof described, but by another such which goes like this: ‘What would you advise the Athenians about? About something that you know and think you understand, like wrestling or playing the cithara or writing? For these you learned. But they don’t hold assemblies about these matters or debate them – or if they do, not about how one should play the cithara or wrestle, but about whether they 25 should welcome (paralambanein) teachers of gymnastics or of the cithara or of 65,1 reading and writing in their city.’ (Thus, for instance, in Homer, Achilles, being a politician, did not prophesy to the Hellenes himself, but advised them to make use of a prophet; and again, Themistocles did not have the triremes built on his own initiative (autos), but proposed the building of a fleet after interpreting the oracle,
5 grants to Tritogeneia a wooden wall... –

And this is appropriate. For higher-level skills don’t do away with those that come under them by pre- empting what belongs to them, but, on the contrary, actually bolster them, with the consequence that philosophy can remain the ‘skill of skills, and science of sciences’, while the skills posterior to it remain intact, and thus can provide them with their principles (arkhai).)

10 ‘So you wouldn’t give advice about what you know and think you understand, for it’s not about these subjects, as we said, that they deliberate. But nor would you about subjects on which you’re ignorant and which you don’t suppose you understand, for simple ignorance is not a cause of error. And nor indeed about matters of which you’re ignorant, but which you imagine you understand; for this is the characteristic of double ignorance: “advice is of the person who understands a subject and not that of a wealthy person”. ’

15 The remaining leg , I mean understanding but thinking one does not understand, or not knowing that one knows, is incoherent; for knowledge, being light, does not escape the notice of the person who has it. Such, then, is the division by means of which Alcibiades is once more convicted of being a poor adviser in respect of his knowledge.

20 Now these three were learned in Athens – reading and writing, playing the cithara, and wrestling – for the organisation of the tripartition of 66,1 the soul, as we said at the beginning; the reason (logos) was organised by means of reading and writing, spirited emotion (thumos) tamed by means of playing the cithara, and desire (epithumia) strengthened and made tough by wrestling. And he adds that ‘You refused to practice the flute.’ There were a number of reasons that they did not cultivate the study of the flute: first, because this 5 has to do with ecstasy and has more to do with inspiration and not with education. For in cithara-playing, it is possible to use reasoned speech (logos) as well, but in flute-playing that is not at all the case: not only is himself unable to use speech or to sing, but he can’t even hear someone else singing, for this is a noisy ; which is why we talk about ‘citharasong’, but not ‘flute-song’. And Athena threw away her flute on this account, as 10 an impediment to reason (logos). (The goddess is the overseer of wisdom. as the poets say, it was because she saw that her face looked unbecoming. Or perhaps this is to be understood in the following way: that ‘the face of sound is language’, but the flute is hostile to it.) Also, the poet is always attributing cithara-playing to the Hellenes, but nowhere portrayed them playing the flute; but to the Trojans, 15 as they are foreigners, he assigned the flute, and he also said of them that
the Trojans came on with clamour and cry like birds...’

And it was appropriate that he assign the flute to these people, since they are 67,1 Phrygians – for reportedly the flute was invented in Phrygia, in the context of mysteries and inspirations. There too Marsyas, who competed in music with Apollo and was bested, he using a flute, the other a cithara. And Alcibiades himself said about the Thebans, ‘Let the children of the Thebans play the flute, because they don’t know how to have a conversation.’

That is the content of the survey (theôria). Come on, then: I say that you intend... We should investigate why Socrates examines the young man based on knowledge alone, and not on the other criteria .

We say, then, that he could not do so on the basis of his ability to express 10 himself, because he knew that he had this from Pericles, with whom he had lived earlier, as a consequence he was a natural (tên phusin) orator. And on the basis of good intentions (prohairesis) either: for was good on account of his immunity to the affection of caring for money, his generosity with his possessions, and the fact that he looked down on his other lovers. Well, then, as you were about to mount the podium... Since he is addressing a person with oratorical aspirations (rhêtorikos), he uses rhetorical jargon throughout, as he does here. He furnishes with an audience and a theatre, you see, and lays out the podium (bêma) with rushing toward it, and he adds himself as the bit , so that he can rein in the young man’s affections and his passionate longing to advise : for he says, ‘Supposing I took you aside and asked...’ 20 Is it something that you understand better than they do? Here is the first premiss, that ‘The good adviser knows the subject of his advice better than those whom he is about to advise: since his knowledge isn’t worse, for that would be crazy; nor is it equal, for that would be useless.’ Now the only things you know are what you’ve learned from others 25 or discovered yourself... the second premiss, that ‘The one who knows better either learned or discovered ’: for understanding is twofold, as we have learned. Is that right? Would you have wanted to investigate or learn ? the third premiss, that ‘The person who has learned or discovered something, either investigated it or was taught: the latter are the means, the former the ends.’ (By ‘being taught’ here, one should understand ‘learn’ ). 68,1 So there was a time when you didn’t think you knew... the fourth and final premiss, that ‘the person who has investigated or been taught something is able to state the time when he did not think he knew it’.

We should understand that the prosyllogism is in the first figure, the syllogism in the second figure. For here is the prosyllogism: ‘The good 5 adviser knows better about the subject of his advice than those whom he advises; such a person either learned or discovered ; such a person either investigated or was taught; such a person is able to state a time when he did not think he knew; therefore the good adviser is able to state the time when he did not think he knew ’ And the syllogism, assuming the last proposition demonstrated in the prosyllogism, 10 proceeds in the second figure as follows: ‘The good adviser is able to state a time when he did not think he knew; Alcibiades is not able to state the time when he did not think he knew; therefore Alcibiades is not a good adviser.’ (We should understand that himself unfolded the syllogism at greater length, but we re- organised it into syllogistic form.) 15 Actually, I myself know just about everything that you have learned... He was right to add ‘just about’ (skhedon ti): for it’s likely that Alcibiades was aware of some knick- knack (skeuarion) in his house that Socrates didn’t know about! But you didn’t want to learn flute-playing... True enough: , you see, is the one who said of the Thebans, ‘let the children of the Thebans play the flute, because they don’t understand how to converse’. But I don’t think you have been , either by night or by day, on your excursions from home... That is, ‘You did not learn anything other than these subjects, assuming you never escaped my notice.’ This resembles what Diomedes says to Athena, when he tells her, ‘Nor do I escape your notice when I move’. For Socrates was always present with Alcibiades, like our conscience, which attends each of our actions. Well, then, is it when the Athenians take counsel about reading and writing...? Here begins the second refutation, which we reduced to a division, to the effect that advice either concerns what he knows and thinks he understands, or what he does not know, but thinks he understands, or what he does not know and does not think he understands; 69,1 and we stated that the fourth, and incoherent, leg is to know, but think one does not know. For each and every one of these alternatives, we have demonstrated that it is impossible for him to be a good adviser. But the text mentions only two, namely, that he knows and thinks that he knows (and about these the Athenians never deliberate in assembly, 5 if in fact has only learned cithara-playing, wrestling, and reading and writing), and things he doesn’t know about and knows he doesn’t know about (for adds that ‘you also will not advise them about housebuilding’, and Alcibiades, who is ignorant about this, knows that he does not know). I presume it won’t be house-building... We should understand that it is not 10 because advice about house-building has a low value that Socrates said ‘Then you will not give advice when they deliberate about house-building’, but rather because Alcibiades is ignorant about house-building. (For he added that ‘The house-builder will surely advise better about this than you will?’, meaning he ‘will give accurate advice about what pertains to house-building’.) To guard against that , he also introduced an example from a 15 skill with more status (with the words, ‘nor surely when about prophecy’), to show that it is not the status or lack of status of a subject that makes one equipped (or not equipped) to give advice, but accurate knowledge of the matters at hand. For as also mentions next, ‘Giving advice, I think, belongs to the person who knows about each subject, and not to 20 the wealthy person’. Nor will they be taking counsel about prophecy... The prophetic skill is twofold in Plato, one kind being a kind of madness, as he says in the Phaedrus, and this is inspired and divine; the other is, so to speak, ‘investigative’ and ‘searching’, which is indeed a ‘skill’ – about which he says now, that ‘about this the prophet will advise better than you’. For no one will give advice about the former , since it is not teachable.

With the god’s favour
