Lecture 13
With the god’s favour
Soc. Now tell me: are you saying that some just things are advantageous, 115A– but others are not?

The present dialogue has ten syllogisms; he lays out the fifth of these to prove 25 that the just and the advantageous are one and the same. He uses two syllogisms to demonstrate this: first, that everything just is also advantageous; next, that 115,1 everything advantageous is also just. For converting yields the identity .

Now, he presents the syllogism as follows: ‘Everything just is noble (kalon): and everything noble is advantageous: therefore everything just is advantageous’. And the youth does not reject the minor premiss (the one stating that ‘everything just is noble’), as someone who cares about his reputation (hôs philotimos), because he considers just deeds praiseworthy. (That is also why he donated ten talents to the council of his own free will). But he resists the major premiss (the one stating that ‘everything noble is advantageous’), by arguing that some deeds are noble but bad, while other, shameful deeds are good. And this isn’t a contradiction. For there are two contradictories: noble and shameful, and good and bad – and the noble is contradictory to the shameful, while the good is contradictory to the bad, but the noble is not contradictory to 10 the bad. For (as claims) a noble act can be a bad one: for instance, going to war on behalf of one’s country, and dying for a friend (philos) – this action is noble because it’s praiseworthy (for it’s done for a friend), but it’s not good, inasmuch as it brings no benefit to the body. And the converse holds of the shameful and the good, as in the case of refusing to give one’s life for a friend.
Now the Oracle made both of these points very clear. On the topic of refusing to give one’s life for a friend, on the one hand, said this:
15 You did not defend your friend, though you were at his side as he was dying: You arrive impure: depart from my all-beautiful shrine.
116,1 On the other hand, when it came to a man who thrust out his arm to help his friend, but his spear struck , she said this:
You reached out to save your companion: the blood does not pollute you, but you are purer of slaughter than you were before.

Now might have refuted Alcibiades by saying the following: ‘But the human being is the soul, and harms (kaka) to the instrument don’t come back on its user. It’s true that harms suffered by parts do come back on the whole: if, then, the human being were compounded from soul and body, then harms to the body would come back on the whole. But since the one 10 is the instrument and the other is its user, the errors (hamartêmata) of the instrument can’t come back on its user, just as the blunting of the adze doesn’t come back on its user’. But since these are more philosophical (and the question would be begged right from the start, ‘On what grounds that the human being is the soul?’), he employs three arguments to prove that the just and the advantageous are one the same: and the first argument is that everything noble is advantageous.

The first argument runs as follows: ‘Two – say, nobility 15 (to kalon) and harm (to kakon) – don’t both attend on a single – say, courage. Rather, two attend on two . For nobility attends courage on behalf of one’s friend, but harm attends death: so courage and death are not identical, at least, not unless everyone who is brave in battle dies, or everyone who dies in battle is brave. The consequence is that the two – both the harm of death, and nobility – attend two and not one, courage’. And in saying this, 20 allows that death is something harmful, since he is crafting his words for Alcibiades.

The second argument: ‘Even if we do grant that two (nobility and the harm of death) follow courage as such, nonetheless, they don’t follow in the same way: for nobility followed courage insofar as it is courage , but harm only followed by accident, by the 25 destruction of the underlying and by allowing courage as such . For if one had destroyed courage insofar as it is courage, it would have been cowardice that followed for that person, not death; for it’s cowardice that destroys courage as such’.

117,1 Next, since he is conversing not in the Socratic manner, but as a teacher, and thus he is overstepping the instruction of the god, according to which ‘the god made me a midwife , but prevents me from begetting’ (for now he is teaching these lessons, rather than acting as a midwife, since we would need to hear these statements from Alcibiades, not asserted by Socrates), and since he was a midwife’s son, he reverses the arrangement, and 5 makes Alcibiades the respondent by asking these same questions of Alcibiades. And he practices the argument with courage, since their conversation has taken a turn toward military matters; and he proves that courage is good, since it is something noble. (For consider, if he had been talking with Charmides, the ‘most temperate’ (sôphronestatos) – since that dialogue was actually entitled by him ‘Charmides, or Concerning Temperance’ – he would have practised the argument with temperance ).

10 He asks him, then, ‘whether you would choose to be a coward, or to die?’ And Alcibiades chooses to die, since he is courageous. And again, ‘Do you consider death and cowardice equally ’? And Alcibiades also agrees here, in error: for it is better to die than to be a coward, since courage causes us to exist well (eu einai), but life exist: surely, too, the drop (apoptôsis) is worse than the other, that is, existing in a bad condition 15 (kakôs) than not existing. But since these matters are more philosophical, Socrates lets them go and uses own words to prove that everything noble is good.

Now earlier on, before his midwifery, proved that everything noble is good in the following way: ‘Courage is something noble’ (for the young man granted this also in the case of justice); ‘everything noble, insofar as it is noble, 20 is good’ (for the second syllogism showed this, the one which asserted that ‘the good followed courage insofar as it is courage, since it is noble, and it was in an accidental way that death, which is harmful, followed something noble); ‘and since the phrase “insofar as” implies convertibility , it is also noble insofar as it is good. And after we have made the same 25 arguments in the case of temperance’, he says, ‘and the other excellences (aretai), we will hold that everything noble, insofar as it is noble, is good, and thereby the same’.

Following his midwifery, however, he devises a different kind of syllogism, asserting that ‘Courage is desirable to Alcibiades; everything desirable is good, 118,1 since desire waxes and wanes with the good (for the greater the good, the greater the desire); courage, then, is good; and the same goes for the other excellences; the consequence is that everything noble is good’. For if courage, as something noble, is desirable, and if it is also an object of love (erastos) (for 5 what’s noble and beautiful (kalon) is so relative to love), and if the desirable is good, then courage is good; and after we have done the same for self-control and proven that self-control is something good, and likewise for the other excellences, we will hold that everything noble is good, as we have said. And since the particular assertion is convertible with itself, and it’s been proven that everything noble (and the aggregate constructed from the particular assertions) is good, the entire aggregate is also convertible.

In addition to this, he also uses a third syllogism to prove that everything <noble> is good, and the converse: he has employed a proof that Aristotle found use for in On the Heavens . That is, after he takes two contradictory terms (and each of their legs is convertible with the other leg), he proves that the terms on the diagonal cannot both be true. And here are 15 the two contradictory terms : generated, ungenerated; destructible, indestructible. Now, since he has demonstrated that the generated is convertible with the destructible (for everything generated is destructible, and vice versa), and likewise for the other pair (everything ungenerated is indestructible, and everything indestructible ungenerated), it’s impossible for both of the diagonal 20 terms to hold true , e.g., destructible and ungenerated: for if both do hold true, then – since he has proven that everything destructible is generated – there will be something generated and ungenerated, and a contradictory proposition will hold.
This is the proof that Plato has used here, taking the following as his two contradictory terms: good, harmful; noble, shameful.

And once he has proven that the good is convertible with the noble and the harmful with the shameful, he shows that it’s impossible for one and the same 25 thing to be both noble and harmful. For if it is, then, since he has proven that the noble is good, one and the same thing will be both good and bad, which is impossible.

That is the content of the survey. 119,1 Now tell me: are you saying that some just things are advantageous, but others are not? What is the object (skopos) of the discussion (praxis)? To show, using three arguments, that the just and advantageous are one and the same: and he does this by the convertibility of the just and the advantageous. And notice that he did not ask whether he thought that no just things 5 were advantageous, but instead he posed the more persuasive question, whether he thought that some just thing was advantageous, but another was not. And he introduces that syllogism, that ‘everything just is noble’, and grants this: but he resists the major , which states ‘and everything noble is advantageous’. What do you mean by that question? The young man wasn’t unsure without 10 cause, but because Socrates named two things, the just and the advatangeous, and then asked whether some of these are noble but others shameful, was unsure to which of these to refer his answer. Have you ever thought that someone was doing something that was both just and shameful? Notice how he asks him for the minor , and the young man, since he’s fond of reputation (philotimos), grants that everything just is noble. 15 some noble are harmful. Notice how he resists the major premiss, that not everything noble is good, considering wounds suffered in war. Surely you call a rescue of this sort noble? He could certainly have said the same things about temperance (sophrosûnê), but since this discussion is about warcraft, he mentioned a relevant example. (Consider, the temperance of Hippolytus was noble, but not good, since he died). Now courage is one thing, but death is something else, right? Here is the first solution, that two follow from two , not two from one: for courage and death are not the same. 120,1 Now let’s see whether, insofar as it’s noble, it’s also good... Here is the second syllogism, the one which says, ‘Even if we allow that both nobility and the harm of death follow on one and the same act, namely courage, it’s still not in the same way ; rather, the noble follows from courage insofar as it is courage, while harm follows accidentally, by letting 5 go free and attacking its underlying subject ’. That is why he says: ‘Consider <whether>, insofar as it is noble, it is also good’ (and he uses this phrase ‘insofar as’ (hêi) in cases of convertibility), ‘following our current model of courage. For it was claimed earlier that two results follow on two , but now that two follow on one: for nobility 10 in and of itself follows courage, but harm follows incidentally. So consider whether this nobility itself is good or bad’. Consider it like this: which would you rather have, good things or bad things? He changes the structure of the argument to midwifery, to avoid overstepping the injunction of the god: ‘the god made me a midwife , but prevents me from begetting’ . And he sets the argument out for 15 Alcibiades as follows, saying that ‘courage is desirable; everything desirable is good (because these two wax and wane together; for we have greater desire for the greater good); courage, then, is good’.

And after we have practised the same arguments in the case of the other noble , since nobility is a collection of excellences – for example, in the 20 case of temperance: ‘for the temperance of Hippolytus is harmful incidentally, since death followed’ – <we will conclude that everything noble is good>. on a par with death... Notice how the young man errs here: for existing in a bad condition is worse than not existing. rescuing your friends in battle ... Here begins the 25 first dialectical proof, to the effect that two follow on two acts, that is, nobility from courage and harm from death, through midwifery. 121,1 So we may fairly describe each of these acts as follows: the second dialectical argument, to the effect that ‘the noble, insofar as it is noble, is good’. Isn’t it also noble insofar as it’s good? He employs conversion here, because (since the phrase ‘insofar as’ is used in cases of convertibility) is also noble insofar as it is good. noble, but harmful... At this point he presents the third syllogism, the one that develops from two contradictories, which Aristotle also found useful. And he explains that that ‘in saying that the noble act is harmful, you are not uttering a contradiction on the face of it, but you are potentially contradicting yourself, since what you’re saying is actually that the harmful is good, given that the noble is convertible with the good, and everything noble is good’.
Lecture 14
With the god’s favour
Soc. Now then, let’s take a new approach: people who act nobly do things 116B– well, don’t they?

Since Socrates demonstrated that everything noble is good, using the example of courage (since he was explaining how ‘the noble, insofar as it is noble, is desirable; everything desirable is good; therefore, everything noble is good’), and Alcibiades granted that courage is noble, courage is therefore good. And 15 once we have established the same result for the other excellences (since nobility is, in a sense, a collection and flowering of the excellences), we will also conclude that everything noble is good.

Now since he knew (even before Aristotle) that a demonstration relying on particular terms is weak, he wants to demonstrate this conclusion using a universal argument as well: so he takes universal propositions, and uses these to demonstrate that everything noble is good and the converse. And the syllogism goes like this: ‘The person who performs noble deeds, acts 20 well; the person who acts well has well-being (eudaimonia); the person who has well-being does good deeds; therefore, the person who performs noble deeds performs good deeds, and through this, it follows that the noble is good’.

122,1 Since Plato has advanced these arguments, people who want to disparage this syllogism enjoy a great deal of license for criticism, asking ‘What differentiates the premisses from each other? That is, what differentiates “performing noble deeds” from “acting well”? Or what differentiates “acting well” from “well-being”?’

Well, we reply to the first question that ‘performing noble deeds (kala)’ 5 and ‘acting well’ are not the same. For ‘well’ is a middle term between the good, and the noble or beautiful (kalon), since ‘well’ is an outflowing and a kind of radiance of the good toward the beautiful (kalon), beginning from the good, and ending with the beautiful. For that reason, the beautiful is also described by the ‘well’, for example when we say that those who speak beautifully speak well. But ‘well’ also refers to the good, since we also describe people 10 who are kind to us and wish us good things as ‘well-intentioned’ (eunous) toward us.

‘Well’ applies to each because it is desirable. The beautiful, of course, is desirable because it calls to itself (kaloun eph’ heauto), while the good (agathon) because it causes all people to ‘rush with energy’ (agan thein) toward it. That is also why the extraordinary (daimônios) Aristotle conjectured as the first cause, not the first principle (arkhê), but , mind (nous). And when he discussed it in the Metaphysics, he described ‘well’ as twofold, 15 applying in one sense to the military leader (stratêgos), and in the other to his army, and ‘wellness’ in the leader causes ‘wellness’ in the army. In this way, ‘well’ became assimilated with beauty, since beauty is akin to Intellect (nous). For had his argument been made about the good, he would not have used ‘well’, because the first stands above this.

And as for the second question, this is not the same, for it is one thing to act well and another to achieve well-being (eudaimonein): for the former befits 123,1 self-moved agents (since it is a distinguishing feature of self-movement to live with excellence ), but well-being has reached us from above, if we are beings who have lived in an excellent way; for the radiance that shines from divinity attends those who have made themselves suitable , and this radiance is well-being, and this kind of movement deriving from another (heterokinêtos) is greater than self-movement; for being led by divinity is superior to being led by their own selves.

Next, he attaches two premisses to what’s been said so far, and thus draws the conclusion that was proposed at the outset – one more general , and one more specific. The more specific premiss is that the person who performs good deeds, performs advantageous deeds (for the good and advantageous are the same); and the more general is that the person who does just things, does noble things (for Alcibiades was already committed 10 to this, that ‘everything is just is noble’); and concludes that ‘surely everything just is also advantageous’.

Next, he converts one of the premisses stated in the middle, by saying that ‘the person who acts well also performs noble deeds’. And he accomplishes this by proving that all of the premisses convert, and on that account, the conclusion 15 also follows. For it had been proposed to prove not only that everything just is advantageous, but also that everything advantageous is just, so that this conversion would follow: ‘The advantageous is good: the good causes well-being: what causes well-being constitutes good action: it is such to perform noble deeds; to behave thus constitutes justice; therefore, the advantageous is just’.

20 Now after Socrates’ argument has proceeded that way, and after Alcibiades has been released from double ignorance (but he has not yet reached simple ignorance: rather, he is in the borderlands (methorios) between double and simple ignorance), grants that he does not know what sorts of statements he is agreeing to, one kind or another. For he says, ‘I have no idea what I’m saying (ho ti legô)... one moment things seem like this to me, and at another moment, they seem different’ . And this lies between 25 simple ignorance (namely, knowing that one does not know) and double ignorance (namely, firmly supposing that one knows), that is, supposing at one moment that one knows, and at another not holding that supposition (just as opinion is a mean between double ignorance and knowledge. For the person holding an opinion who knows that it is so, but remains ignorant of why it is so, is so to speak ‘in the borderlands’ between those cases that are diametrically contrary to one another). That is also why the argument was being made that the person holding a opinion differs from the knowledgeable person only in respect of the reason why: for he does exactly what the knowledgeable person does, just as the empirical doctor does exactly what the scientific doctor does.

Next, since Socrates wants to free Alcibiades completely from double 5 ignorance, he attacks it and condemns it with dramatic flair (ektragôidei), claiming that it is the cause of our going astray (planê), the cause of error, the most shameful and ugly thing of all (aiskhistotatos). That’s because simple ignorance is ‘most shameful’ (aiskhistos), but this is ‘the most shameful thing of all’ (aiskhistotatos) and ‘the most deserving of reproach’. That’s why it belongs to to be ‘most deserving of reproach’, since it’s the cause of our wandering astray: this follows from the fact that the person who knows the path doesn’t go astray, nor does the person who, 10 while not knowing , recognises his ignorance (for this person would not even undertake the journey); but it’s the person who is ignorant, while at the same time supposing he knows, . And he is the cause of ethical mistakes (hamartêmata) as well: for this person tries to teach others what he doesn’t understand, and instills damaging beliefs in them.

Now, describes as ‘the most shameful thing of all’, since even simple ignorance counts as ‘shameful’, as it is a form of ignorance. For ignorance produces a shameful effect (aiskhos) in the soul; but shame is one thing, and disease is something else. For shame is observed in reason (logos) alone, but ethical weakness (ponêria), which is a disease of the soul, does not belong only to one of its parts, like reason (for disease does not belong in one part , as Hippocrates says: ‘for if a human being were one , he would not suffer pain’); rather, it lies in the struggle between the parts of the soul.

125,1 And this is ‘the most shameful thing of all’ because we are doubly ignorant, and it’s ‘most deserving of reproach’, considering that we do not reproach those who lack , but those who have it but fail to use it, or those who use it badly. Likewise, the simple lack of knowledge (amathia) ‘deserves reproach’, since the person who lacks knowledge, despite possessing 5 innate principles of reason (logoi) as part of his nature, fails to put those arguments to use; but it is ‘most deserving of reproach’ when someone possesses and puts them to bad use, and this applies in the case of double lack of knowledge.

And it ‘produces the most harm’ (kakourgotatos), since it strives to draw false conclusions and to persuade us of what it doesn’t know. And the person who is in this condition has fallen short of Soul (psukhê) and Intellect (nous) and God (theos). First, due to his double lack of knowledge, he has fallen short of Soul, since understanding (gnôsis) is congenial 10 to the soul; and due to his being in a ‘most shameful’ condition, he has fallen short of Intellect, since he is unable to revert to himself, which is distinctive of mind, and also because the noble or beautiful (kalon) is congenial to Intellect, and thus in becoming ‘most shameful’ he has fallen short of it; and he has fallen short of God in ‘producing the most harm’ and ‘deserving reproach’, since simplicity is congenial to God, and wellness (to eu) also derives from simplicity. (For ‘well’ is a designation of simplicity, which is why we call simple ways ‘well-intentioned’ (euêtheis)).

15 ‘And how will you offer advice, Alcibiades – you who desire a good reputation – though you deserve reproach? And when you desire to be the most beautiful and noble (kallistos), though you are the most shameful and ugly (aiskhistos)? And when you desire to know what’s advantageous and advise it, though you are the most harmful?’ We should understand <that> it is by being most deserving of reproach that falls short of God, and thereby (hôs) of being blessed; for the word ‘blessed’ was used of a person untouched by the doom of 20 death, which is also why ‘reproachable’ is opposed to ‘blessed’ in the line :
That blessed man – and I do not reproach his fortunes...

That is the content of the survey. Now let’s take yet another approach... By using the word ‘yet’, he shows that 126,1 he intends to produce the same again using a different argument. For before, he produced this conclusion in particular terms, but now in universal terms. People who do what’s noble act well, don’t they? He asserts the first premiss, that those who perform noble deeds act well. Just because he makes the 5 just and advantageous identical by using the intermediate term ‘noble’, he does not thereby mean that they are absolutely (antikrus) the same (for the nature of the good is one thing, and that of the noble, something else; after all, the good has transcended the noble or beautiful (kalon) ‘above’, and ‘below’ on account of matter, which is shameful, but participates in the good). Rather, that they are convertible in the case of a human being, since they convert in their subject. It’s like when we say that ‘the human being’ differs in no respect from ‘the being who is capable of laughter’: that’s not because they are the same thing, but because the subject possesses the property of ‘humanity’ in every case where ‘capable of laughter’ is predicated of it; hence, these are also convertible in the case of a human being.

And since justice in a human being embraces goodness as well, it’s clear, considering his earlier discussion of courage, that is good; and here he comments that those who perform noble deeds act well, and according 15 to this account, they have well-being and thereby are performing good deeds, and acting, well-being, and acting well are functions of souls. It’s also clear in the passage that he maintains the identity of the noble and good ‘according to this argument, at least’, meaning ‘they are the same with reference to the subject, in that the subject escapes neither’.

This is also the view of the philosopher Proclus: but Damascius interprets differently, taking the view that just because the noble, just, and advantageous are the same with respect to their subject, it does not follow that they are the same with respect to their distinguishing character (idiotês), but rather, they are convertible in spite of remaining separate with respect to their own distinguishing character, and it’s insofar as they are convertible that they are called ‘the same’. As he explains, it’s like how the excellences (aretai) are 25 mutually convertible while they separately preserve their own distinguishing character. For consider, the convertibility of the excellences doesn’t cause them to be identical , nor does the convertibility of ‘capable of laughter’ and ‘human’, but following conversion each retained its 127,1 proper, distinctive character. Thus the good and the beautiful are also not the same, even if they do convert. And that is why the passage says ‘everything else like this’, meaning ‘things that are identical in their subject, but differ in their unique character (idiotês)’. And people who act well possess well-being (eudaimonia), don’t they? Here is the second premiss: we have noted the puzzles (aporiai) that confront it, as well as their solutions. And they get these because they act well and admirably? didn’t combine these terms – ‘acting well’ and ‘acting admirably’ – at random, but because well is a mean between the beautiful and the good, and well flowed from the good to the beautiful, and serves as a bond between them. That’s why , who knows all of this, 10 uses the words ‘therefore well is good’, even though the conclusion ought to assert ‘therefore the person who acts well does good deeds’. Surely good conduct is noble? Notice how he converts one premiss here, providing us with an idea (ennoia) of how to convert the others, and also on this account that everything advantageous <is just>: for that is what demanded proof. For consider, he made the conversion 15 by saying, ‘Good conduct is noble’. So we’ve seen once again that they’re the same... He didn’t say ‘once again’ idly, but because this had already been proven by the syllogism based on particular terms, but now has been proven using the universal premiss. So it follows that if we find something noble, we’ll also find that it’s good – according to this argument, at least. Notice how well the interpretation of the philosopher Proclus accords with this passage. For he says that ‘everything that we find noble, we’ll also find good’, he means that ‘ are convertible through their subject’. For no feature of the subject that is good escapes being just. We should be grateful to the philosopher for explaining these things in this way. 25 Well then, are good things advantageous? At this point, he adds the other two premisses: first, the more specific premiss, that ‘good are advantageous’, and later the more general premiss, that ‘as has granted, just 128,1 are noble’. And on this basis, everything just is advantageous, and vice versa. So, Alcibiades, just things are advantageous... Since he introduced the conclusion , it is appropriate that he also mentioned Alcibiades’ name, in order to arouse his attention and show him that he is the one offering these 5 , and not Socrates. Well then, aren’t you the one who is making these points? ‘So who gave these answers and offered these ? Aren’t you the one who is giving the answers?’ Because, as has often been pointed out, the person who gives the answers is the speaker, not the person who asks the questions. So if someone were to stand up to advise... If it was any other writer who was saying all this, rather 10 than Socrates, he would certainly have addressed Alcibiades with vulgar language following his refutation (elenkhos), saying ‘Now how in the world do you propose to give advice about what you don’t understand?’ But since Socrates is the speaker, what he says to him is this: ‘Surely, if someone stood up to offer advice about what he did not understand, you would laugh at him as he stood up?’ He has put the person who is being ridiculed in the position of 15 laughing at others. For it is the fruit of Socrates’ company to make the person who laughs at others into an object of ridicule himself.

He uses the phrase ‘even the Peparethians’ because Peparethus was an insignificant island; by this, he shows that the famous name of Attica will not help to make the person who is ‘doubly ignorant’ about justice knowledgeable on the subject. ‘For advice is given by the person with understanding about each subject’, not by the person an Athenian; so it’s useful to make this point here. I swear by the gods, Socrates, Notice how the 129,1 young man has been liberated from his double ignorance and has come to stand in the intermediate position: for he claims that ‘one moment things seem like this to me, and at another moment, they seem different’. And the timing of his oath is not without significance; in fact, it shows that he is in a speechless state. (Consider, why did he not swear earlier?) That is also why, when Socrates criticises him, he calls him ‘friend’; another reason is that climbed 5 up one rung : for he stepped from double ignorance into the intermediate condition between simple and double . If someone asked you whether you had two or three eyes... Here, he wants to show that ’ ignorance has put him at odds with himself. And he has deployed quite a few examples that are appropriate to this purpose, by saying ‘if someone asked you if you had the ability to ascend to heaven...’ ; and 10 there’s a sense in which this was appropriate to Alcibiades, on account of Pericles, who used to be called ‘Olympian’. Thus the line went about him,
He hurled the lightning, he thundered, he cast Greece into turmoil...

And it wasn’t thanks to good deeds that gained this respect, but for money, as we learned from the outspoken comedy : he started the 15 Peloponnesian War in order to avoid rendering accounts of the money spent on Pheidias’ Athena. ‘Again, if someone asked you about navigation, how would you answer? Or about cooking? Yet in these cases you aren’t at odds with yourself, since you know that you are ignorant’.

These examples also are appropriate: the first , because it shows that it’s necessary for the statesman to be raised above those entrusted to his care; and the next case of the navigator because, just as the navigator exercises foresight on behalf of his ship, must exercise foresight on behalf of those entrusted to his care, even if he is above them; and the third case of cooking, because it’s necessary for the statesman to be gentle (prosênês) to those he advises in making his arguments. For if those he advises failed to be persuaded that their adviser is guiding them 130,1 for their own benefit, they would never be persuaded by him. For it’s through gentleness alone that the Greeks’ adviser was called
one from whose tongue flows speech sweeter than honey.

Now, does not ask questions that admit of possibilities, but questions with an impossible answer. For he didn’t ask ‘whether you have 5 two eyes or one’ – since would have been possible, and could have given different answers at different times; but whether he has three eyes, or two or four hands. I’m a little worried about myself now... Alcibiades is afraid of answering even such a clear question. And this is for someone who has been 10 shown the abundance of Socrates’ dialectical power: that is, it’s because he’s already had experience of this that he is afraid. ‘For those of the Argives who have been struck, they understand’, as the saying goes. , his soul will necessarily waver about it... At this point, since Alcibiades has been loosely (pakhumerôs) benefited, Socrates launches an assault on double ignorance and makes all 15 those points against it a little later. Don’t you realise, then, that the errors in our conduct (hamartêmata en têi praxei) are caused by this kind of ignorance, The phrase ‘through this kind of ignorance’ (dia tautên 131,1 tên agnoian) was well chosen, since our errors of reason arise through ignorance. (And presently we are examining cognitive errors (kata gnôsin), where we speak of double and simple ignorance. But there is also another source of errors, namely, force: that is, errors fall into two categories, 5 arising either by ignorance, or by force). Now at this point he proves that is a cause of errors as well . For those who have knowledge do not err, since they succeed in their goal; nor do those in simple ignorance, since they do not make the attempt in the first place. And ignorance (amathia) that deserves reproach... That is, it fell short of the good because it was deserving of reproach. For reproachability is contrary to blessedness, and blessedness is appropriate to the gods, for whom the doom 10 of death does not exist. Well then, can you name anything more important than the just and noble? He says that the just and good and advantageous are of ‘the greatest importance (megista)’, since all people strive to make use of these from birth, working from a common concept; it’s unlike other skills, where certain people possess in separation . For example, certain people – not all – 15 make use of the art of letters (grammatikê), or of philosophy, but all people endeavour to encourage and discourage and praise and blame and denounce and defend , and in short, make use of the three kinds of rhetoric. And orators do not differ from other people, except in the arrangement or lack of arrangement : one says the same thing, whether or not one speaks with competence in the skill . Hence, he says that these ‘greatest’ matters are universal. So this belongs to rhetoric alone, just as speaking Greek belongs to all Greeks, but skilfully causing someone to speak Greek belongs to the art of letters alone.
Lecture 15
With the god’s favour
Oh dear, Alcibiades, what suffering (pathos) you’ve been through...118B–

Consider that there are two parts of the soul, one concerned with cognition, the other with vital functions: the cognitive part is purified by cross-examination, but the vital part is purified by forceful correction (epiplêxis). Therefore, after Socrates has purified the cognitive of Alcibiades by proving to him that he suffers from double ignorance, he the vital 5 part by explaining – with tragic flair (ektragôidêsai) – all the different kinds of troubles that follow from double ignorance (for he described the cause of his errors (hamartêmata) as ‘the most shameful thing of all, most deserving of reproach, most harmful’ ). At this point, after laying out the qualities of double ignorance in general, he goes on to mention its individual (idia) consequences to Alcibiades, by saying, ‘Oh dear, Alcibiades ’ . Now, this is the of someone 10 who is mourning and bemoaning Alcibiades as if he has perished, making a speech about the departed. This is Pythagorean : for the Pythagoreans used to cast out unsuitable from their company (homakoeion) with their belongings, make a funeral monument (kenotapheion) for them, and mourn them and speak of them as if about the departed.
Also, when he says ‘what’ (hoion), in ‘what suffering you’ve been through’, it’s similar to the tragic verse:
There’s nothing so terrible to describe,

133,1 Which I hesitate to call by name: As appropriate to suppressing , he raises the tone of his cross-examination, that is: ‘it is undiscovered, beyond fate, unspeakable’. And it’s appropriate, too, that he said ‘I hesitate to call it by name’, since it is unspeakable (aphrastos) and cannot be captured by language (arrhêtos), inasmuch as this has to do with matter (hulê), just as matter itself cannot be captured by language and is without form (aneideos). Granted, the 5 first cause is also beyond language, but that is as beyond form: matter, on the other hand, is beyond language because it is inferior to all form. Nonetheless, since we two are alone, it must be said: Because public criticism is interpreted as hostility by a person who is in the habit of caring about their reputation. That’s also why a certain Pythagorean, criticised in public by his teacher, could not bear the shame and killed himself. Hence among philosophers, the habit used to be to offer criticism in private, not in public. You’re wedded to extreme ignorance, my very good man: ‘Wedded’ (sunoikeis) is a good choice of word. Consider, if the reason that civil strife is worse than war is that the one is waged by people from outside and far apart, but the other is waged by people within and nearby (the saying ‘out of all brotherhood, outlawed...’, etc. is about this), then war between members of the same household is worse than civil strife to the same degree as they are nearer together. And does not only say ‘you’re wedded to ignorance’, but ‘extreme ’. The argument (logos) convicts you of it, and so do you yourself: you have strong witnesses to this, since the argument convicts you (because it’s been shown that in a context of question and answer, the respondent is the speaker, not the questioner); and what’s more, you have an invincible witness, yourself. 15 That’s why you’re rushing into politics... That is, ‘Your beliefs are engendering a way of life in you: since you’re doubly ignorant in supposing you know about justice before you’ve learned about it, you are hurrying into public life’. And you’re not the only one who’s suffered this, but most ... Now to Alcibiades, this is a 135,1 consolation, to share his bad condition with many : but this was no consolation to Socrates, since he wanted all people to be good, since he was the protector of humankind. There are only a few exceptions, among them, perhaps, your guardian 5 Pericles. We inquire why he praises Pericles here, calling him ‘wise’, but runs him down a little later, saying that he is not a statesman (politikos) (just as he also proves in the Gorgias that is no statesman; this is also how he roused Aristides to produce a speech in opposition, due to the arguments in the Gorgias). Now the philosopher Proclus says, ‘He refutes since he is not a man of knowledge (epistêmôn), but accepts him as a man of true belief (orthodoxastikos)’. But the philosopher Damascius rejects this explanation, arguing that the only difference between a person with true beliefs and a person with knowledge lies in grasp of the cause, just as the scientific physician is no different from the empirical physician, since they do exactly the same things in practice: accordingly, if was a man of true belief, he would not have made mistakes (hêmartanen). Hence his own solution of this puzzle is that accepts Pericles as a 15 general (stratêgos), since goal is victory, but rejects him as a statesman, since he did not make his own citizens noble and good (kaloi kai agathoi).

Next, Alcibiades seizes a short pause after his own relative has been commended (so that Socrates does not repeat about Pericles the questions that he asked : ‘How did he become wise, by learning or discovery?’), 20 and he preempts by enumerating his teachers. For was 136,1 Anaxagoras’ pupil in philosophy, and Pythocles’ pupil in music. He continues to raise his teachers, saying ‘Even now, entering on ‘the threshold of old age’, he is studying under the musician Damon’. But replies: ‘And yet this man is no statesman, since he does not have the ability to make his citizens noble 5 and good’. And he was right not to say make...’, because we cannot distinguish who is wise on this basis. For consider: suppose a person were not preoccupied with matters of secondary importance, and suppose that instead he were to occupy himself with purification (katharsis) or contemplation (theôria), when he separates himself from the many (hoi polloi)? What if he were to live the political life, but his comrades were unsuitable to him? So instead, Socrates said, ‘If he was wise, he would have been able to make another 10 person wise: yet he made neither you, nor your brother Clinias, nor his own sons wise’. ( had them by Aspasia of Miletus, who was also his own teacher—for Pericles was taught by a woman, just as Aristippus was taught by his mother.) But if you claimed that ‘Nonetheless, he was a statesman, thanks to the tributes that he brought in ’, this also wouldn’t imply that he was wise. Consider how he gave power to a city that was feverish, although 137,1 he had the ability to transform his own constitution from democracy to meritocracy (aristokrateia). (For the constitution under him was, as the historian puts it, ‘in name a democracy, but in fact the domination of one man’ . And it is suitable that Plato spoke in favour of meritocracy 5 (aristokrateia), but not for kingship (basileia), since Plato regards kingship with suspicion because of the mortality of the person who becomes king. So due to the instability he entrusted his own constitution to many). Yet the law of nature orders that ‘the more you use what’s impure for bodies as their nourishment, the more harm you do’.
With this, the first part of the dialogue is complete, in which refuted Alcibiades both cognitively and with respect to his vital functions.

Well, we reply that he did this in order to accustom his students to despising money; or in order to provide funds to those in need, by taking them from those with plenty; or so that he might balance out the excess wealth and maintain equality by giving to those who had less. For he pretended to take payment, without actually taking it : for this was Zeno, who was good at pretending; this is also why he used to hear himself called ‘double-tongued’, not because he spoke on both opposing sides of an issue, but because he was in the habit of pretense. This is also why, 15 when a certain tyrant asked him who was plotting with him against the tyranny, he pointed out his own bodyguards; when had done away with them, he was easily done away with himself.

You can also see from this that Plato was the first to make a point of refusing fees, since he was Zeno’s contemporary, and Zeno did take fees. But why does philosophy alone not demand fees, although other 20 skills do? Perhaps it is because no other skilled craftsmen claim to make their pupils good people, but only to make them skilled – as doctors produce doctors, and the carpenter produces carpenters. But the philosopher claims to make people good, and in so doing, he hopes not to be treated unfairly by them. Perhaps Plato made a point of refusing fees thanks to his own wealth; that is also why to this day the school’s endowment (diadokhika) is preserved, despite the many confiscations that are taking place.

During the first section , Socrates cross-examined 5 and refuted (elenxas) Alcibiades, proving for the cognitive that he is doubly ignorant, and using tragic flair to explain to the vital the harmful consequences of double ignorance, describing it as ‘the most shameful thing of all, most deserving of reproach, most harmful’ , the reason we go astray (planê), the cause of errors, and on this basis Alcibiades was enlisted for refutation, and used these to lay him low. In the second section, he encourages 10 after his defeat, and rouses him, saying: ‘Be of good hope, Alcibiades: for you have within you something fit for civic knowledge, something fit for ordering the affairs of the state, namely, your commanding part (hêgemonikon): so you ought to take serious, careful foresight (pronoia) for yourself by practicing self-cultivation’. And he encourages him in the present section, which is 15 protreptic , in order that in the final section he can practice midwifery on him and prepare him to declare who the ‘civic person’ really is, namely, the rational soul when it uses the body as an instrument. For this is the definition of the civic person, but the purificatory and 143,1 contemplative person do not use the body as an instrument, since it begins to present an obstacle to them.

But , since he is lazy and concerned with his reputation, says that he doesn’t need to take trouble over self-cultivation, since he does not have to deal with generals who are worthy adversaries: ‘For if I was dealing with superior people, perhaps I would be concerned to surpass them, but since 5 in fact I look to inferior people, there’s no reason to fear that I won’t surpass them: for I have the ability to get the better of them by my own nature’. And because of both these concerns, namely, to avoid going to trouble over self-cultivation, and, for that reason, appearing incapable of setting the affairs of the state in order.

10 But Socrates laments bitterly over him, since in the first place he regards his allies in the contest as his adversaries. For he thinks that his rivals are the Athenian generals, who are really his allies – as if a ship’s pilot were to regard the sailors as his rivals instead of allies, rather than joining them in looking to other adversaries, to the chance movement of the winds and storms. For just as we take care to be 15 healthy and prosper, even if no one knows about it, so too we must take care of ourselves, even if we were to have no rivals to contest with. For our excellence is not measured against others, but against ourselves, and excellence is what it is in and of itself, not relative to something else. For this reason, indeed, we must not turn our attention away to others; and also because, even if it is necessary to look 20 to others, we must not look to many , but to the minority, and they should not be base and ordinary, but good and serious (spoudaios) people.

He also challenges with a counter-factual objection when he says, ‘ even if you don’t look to citizens as adversaries, but as allies, and instead you look to foreigners as really worthy adversaries – 144,1 for example, the Great King of Persia and the kings of the Lacedaemonians, against whom the city of Athens is locked in continual struggles, as the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars demonstrate; but it’s the ancestral custom (patrion) of the Athenians to win by wisdom (sophia)’.

But refuses to retreat from his laziness or his concern for his 5 reputation, but he says that even these people aren’t important. Hence, whereas Socrates, playing up the stature of enemies, once calls them ‘Great King’, and elsewhere ‘Kings of the Lacedaemonians’, Alcibiades calls them ‘the Lacedaemonian generals’, and instead of the ‘Great King’, just ‘king’. But Socrates, 10 who wants him to get free of this sort of combativeness and lazy character, refutes him with an objection and a counterfactual: by way of objection, he says that ‘the greatest enemies against whom our city is locked in continual struggles’, and by way of a counterfactual, he says, ‘even if we were to allow that they aren’t worthy of notice, still, we would have to work on the hypothesis that they were, so that we would be thereby motivated to strive for excellence’. Now, 15 Aristotle in his Protrepticus commented that ‘if we must do philosophy, then we must do philosophy; but if we must not do philosophy, then we must do philosophy; no matter what, then, we must do philosophy’. And Plato says, ‘if the Persian and Lacedaemonian kings are worthy of note, we must attend to 145.1 excellence, so that we might thereby surpass them; but if they aren’t, we must hypothesise that they are, in order that we might strive for excellence; no matter what, then, we must strive for excellence’. And again in the Theaetetus : ‘if Protagoras is lying, he lies; if he is not lying, he lies; no matter 5 what, then, he is lying’. As you can see, we have many arguments along these lines from the philosophers. You also have here the Platonic doctrine, that whereas Aristotle wants Intellect to be the first principle, Plato wants the Good , since intellect lacks the capacity to give a share of itself to a lie, but the good gives a share of itself even to a lie, for there is such a thing as a good lie: likewise here, the notion of taking something untrue as true for the sake of the good. But lying is not intellectual (noeros), as the good is.
Since there are five methods of purification, these five have been transmitted by Plato in the present dialogue. For it is possible to be purified :

By escaping into sacred precincts, or to teachers, or by studying books that 15 one encounters; and he has conveyed this method by saying, ‘But, my blessed friend, trust in me and in the Delphic inscription, “Know Thyself” ’ .

Second, by forceful correction (epiplêxis), which he conveyed when he used the method of rebuking , criticising his cognitive for double ignorance, and his vital part and explaining with tragic flair the consequences of double ignorance, how they are.

20 Third is the Pythagorean , which is also perilous, since it causes one to take a taste of the passions ‘with the tip of the finger’ – which the doctors employ as well, making use of what is ‘a little worse’: and he has conveyed 146,1 this here by saying that ‘You have something in you fitted for ruling the city, your natural leading portion (hêgemonikon), if you find yourself willing to adorn this with education’; for he exalted his reputation-loving nature this way.

Fourth is the Aristotelian , which heals one harm by another (kakôi to kakon iômenos), bringing the battle of the opposites into a harmony; 5 and he has conveyed this here by at one point using an accusation to castigate Alcibiades, and at another time rousing him up to the height with encouragement, causing him to produce the definition of civic knowledge.

Fifth is the most efficacious , the Socratic, which uses a procedure of transformation (metabasis) from similarity; and he uses this here, 10 when he says ‘You long for power? Learn what is true power, which cannot be taken away by a tyrant. You long for pleasure? Learn what is true leisure, which is observed even among the gods’.

20 Following Socrates’ guidance, Alcibiades should have regarded his competitors as worthy of consideration, even if they were not really so, in order that he might take great care to strive for excellence. But since he is lazy, even though 151,1 they actually are worthy, nevertheless he does not regard them as such, in order to avoid the effort of caring for himself. That’s why Socrates also establishes that the Lacedaemonians and Persians are superior to Alcibiades. And he proves this from four arguments: from lineage (and he includes homeland in lineage, for ‘one’s race is also one’s homeland’, as Porphyry puts it); from birth; from upbringing; and from education (and this is divided into two, preparatory education (propaideia) and education proper (paideia)).

from lineage that ‘They derive from Zeus, but you from human beings’: for Perseus was the son of Zeus and Danaë, and Achaemenes was the son of Perseus and Andromeda (the one in heaven), which is also why the Persian are called ‘Achaemenids’. But Alcibiades claims that he himself is also descended from Zeus, for he was 10 originally a descendent of Ajax. And Socrates wittily declares that he too is descended from Zeus, since he was a descendent of Daedalus, and Daedalus traced his line to Hephaestus, the son of Zeus. Now, he claimed that he was Daedalus’ descendent because Daedalus was the first one to separate the feet of statues, which had them together, producing a representation of walking and 15 self-movement (autokinêtos); and Socrates was the first to make humans self-moving, since he did not allow them to come to knowledge by instruction, but 152,1 by midwifery and discovery, and in this way he made them self-moving.

And he says that ‘Even if we are descended from Zeus like are, the lineage is not the same in both these cases: for we watered down our lineage over the intervening generations and we did not maintain its purity, but that’s 5 not their situation; instead, they have guarded this unadulterated in the transmission of their lineage, because they are kings’. And next, he also establishes that they are superior in their homeland, as in their lineage: he says that ‘You are not originally Athenian, Alcibiades, if you trace your lineage from Ajax; for Ajax was from Aegina, and Ajax was from Telamon of 10 Salamis, and it’s from this man that Eurysaces was born’; and that ‘It’s unclear whether you might not really be sprung from Zeus, but illegitimate, since the Athenian women are unguarded’; but the Lacedaemonian women were guarded, as the shameless comedy showed in the line:

153,1 The Lacedaemonians guarded them because they received an oracle that they would have ill fortune if they put forward a king ‘lame in lineage’, that is, one who did not belong to the line of the sons of Heracles. Therefore, when Leotychidas had become king of the Lacedaemonians, because he was a product of adultery they later experienced :’ for 5 Alcibiades, when he joined the Spartans, slept with this man’s mother, the wife of Agis, and that was how he was born. But among the Persians, they did not consider it worthwhile to set a guard , since they felt that the terror of consequent punishments was a sufficient guard.

So much for from lineage (genos); but the argument from birth (genesis) is that among the Persians, from the very beginning, the person who is going to be king grants all his subjects a full display of his own 10 right to rule (basileia). That’s because it was their custom for the eldest to rule; naturally, then, the Persians and all Asia sacrifice to him and pour libations as soon , honouring him as a god (since before Alexander, all Asia was ruled by the Persians). But when Alcibiades was born, not even his neighbours were aware of it.

Next is from upbringing (trophê), that ‘Among those 15 people , as soon as the king was born, the eunuchs with the best reputation began to care for him, and they mould his body parts with an eye to beauty, even making his nose aquiline, showing that the boy is fit for 154,1 leadership and kingship’. (For this is also why the eagle has an aquiline , because it is kingly; and it was due to Cyrus that they began to cultivate the development of this aquilinity, since he was exceptionally kingly and civilised). ‘But when you were born, , you were taken care of by a Thracian slave, who took no care for your beauty; for you have nothing more than your nature as your gift’.

And from education (paideia) is that ‘Those people 5 receive both preparatory education (propaideia) and education (paideia). For after reaching their seventh year, they are taught to hunt not fish and fowl, but four-legged animals; and at the age of fourteen, they identify four tutors for these , one of whom teaches wisdom, another justice, another courage, and another self-control. (Xenophon relates this in his treatment of Persian education). ‘But you studied none of these subjects, except letters, cithara-playing, and wrestling, since Pericles assigned you 155,1 Zopyrus as a tutor, who was physically maimed and rendered useless by old age; and if he weren’t that sort of person, even he wouldn’t be appointed to you and available to you.

But what kinds of excellence (aretê) were the Persians educated in? We assert that it was not the natural forms of excellence (phusikai), since these are not produced by teaching; and they were certainly not the civic (politikai), since would not have said that 5 different men taught different subjects, but one man alone would have been sufficient to teach them all, since they are mutually convertible ; rather, it was the habituated (êthikai) , for these are taught and are not mutually convertible.

But how could Plato be telling the truth when he says here that were educated in wisdom, but later he says to Alcibiades that ‘You have to 10 cultivate yourself, for it’s your city’s ancestral custom (patrion) to win by wisdom (sophia)?’ So if they were educated in wisdom, why does he make a special point of saying this about the Athenians? It’s because the statement (logos) can be true at one time and false at another. For it’s nothing strange if had such a constitution in the distant past, but by the time of Socrates they had declined from this level, and it is no challenge to criticise this constitution . For that reason, the 15 from lineage was also untrue : for Darius, who became king of thanks to a horse’s neigh, was no Achaemenid; so it is the ancient constitution that describes. Alternatively, we might say that perhaps Darius was an Achaemenid, if not as a grandson, still by an indirect line; that is, even if he was not, as the poet says,
20 son, and grandson of Zeus who gathers the clouds;

Socrates has compared Alcibiades with the Persian King and proven him 161,1 inferior to that man , arguing from four distinct : from homeland or lineage, from birth, which he called ‘birthday celebrations’ (genethlia), from upbringing (trophê), and from education (paideia) (and he subdivided education into ‘preparatory education’ and ‘education proper’). Since he did not also compare him with the Lacedaemonian kings and employ the same four arguments to show that he is 5 also inferior to the Lacedaemonians, he now compares the young man with the lifestyle (diaita) and wealth common to both .

Now is generally disgusted (duskherainei) with the criteria of comparison that he uses here for Alcibiades (for if the human being is the soul, we should not make comparisons on these criteria), and he is even more disgusted with the use of wealth as a criterion of comparison, since this 10 especially lies outside of us . For lifestyle (diaita) concerns the body, but wealth concerns what derives from outside ; hence in the case of lifestyle he uses the words ‘if you wish’ but in the case of wealth, ‘we can’t leave this unspoken’ .

He also says, ‘Alcibiades, even if you rejoice in your luxurious lifestyle’ (for Alcibiades was that kind of person, as witness the writers who composed books of many lines about his luxury, just like the cookbooks passed down even today), ‘still the Persian table exceeds your lifestyle, since it is even more luxurious than the Sybaritic table; while if the Lacedaemonians make no use of luxury, you’re still outdone by their frugal lifestyle’. From this passage, raise the 20 puzzle (aporia) why Socrates contrasts Alcibiades with the Persians in luxury; for by doing so, he makes all the more competitive with them, and prone to emulate them in this . Now, we resolve the puzzle as follows, by explaining that ‘nevertheless, he does not compare to the Persians in their soft living alone, but also to the Lacedaemonians, who employ a frugal lifestyle’; moreover, he constructs his argument on the basis of what appears good 25 to Alcibiades, and luxury does seem good to him.

‘But you’re also inferior to the Lacedaemonians in wealth’. Consider that wealth is threefold: self-moving (autokinêtos), moved by another (heterokinêtos), or not moving at all (akinêtos): in every one of these cases the young man is worsted by the wealth of the Lacedaemonians. In the case of unmoved , it’s because after took Messene, 162,1 they marked it offto serve as an abundant resource for their needs; Tyrtaeus the poet said about it,
Messene, good to sow in, good to plant in;
– for the land was fertile.

Moreover, they used to vaunt themselves for their wealth in self-moving , since they enslaved the entire people of the Helots; and was also visibly self-moving, since they were horse-masters, as witness the saying ‘into horse-pasturing Argos’.

They also used to outdo others in wealth that is moved by others (heterokinêtos), since it is reported about them that they demanded two parts of their subjects’ income, and that their veins are said to be ‘of silver and gold’, and there’s the saying ‘Mycenae rich with gold’; and the report of them also 10 runs that the gold entering their possession never left. Hence he also uses a story to describe this kind of tribute: the story goes that once upon a time, a lion who had grown old pretended that he was ill, and the other animals came in to visit him, and he captured them, ate them, and so brought them to ruin. But the fox, who was clever, refused to enter, but 15 instead he stood at the entrance; and when pressed him to come in, he said that he would certainly not, since he observed footsteps of the going in to the , but no footsteps going back out – that is, he saw footsteps going inward from the entrance, but none going back out to the entrance. 163,1 So it is the same in the case of the Lacedaemonians: says that the money goes in, but even to this day, nothing ever goes out. And he compares them to the lion who has grown old, since they live according to a meritocracy (aristokrateia), which is appropriate to the lion, but they weakened it, so that they were at risk of declining from a meritocracy into oligarchy.

5 But if the Lacedaemonians outdo Alcibiades in wealth, the Persian kings outshine Alcibiades far more by this , too. For the story about them runs that entire cities – stretching out as long as a day’s journey – are allocated (aphorizein) for each and every ornament of their women, so that each ornament comes from tribute. That’s also how the cities 10 came to have names derived from these : for where else would get the name ‘Queen’s Girdle’ or ‘Veil’, other than this? And this is not implausible, if you also consider that when Themistocles changed sides the king allocated three cities to supply his needs – for he asked to spend a year among , until he could master Persian customs, and thus to 15 discuss in person his betrayal of Greece – since as the historian relates, handed over Magnesia and Myus and Lampsacus to him.

Now once again raise the puzzle why Socrates plainly discourages Alcibiades from becoming this sort of person, even as he compares him to the Persians, and exalts Persian customs. Well, it’s not that he vaunts their customs; rather, he dismisses them as women, since are lovers of money, having this character thanks to their lower birth – for they are naturally weaker and tend to be fond of money. And since the 5 Persians are like this (effeminate in their character), that’s why they also wear trailing robes and use adornments. And they’re not the only ones like this, but the Indians also have this kind of affection.
Nor does vaunt the Lacedaemonians and express amazement at them, but on the contrary, he reproaches them with the words of the oracle, which runs:
10 Love of money will undo Sparta, and naught else;

And it’s for this reason that Lycurgus mandated that their currency be bronze, and that they steep it in vinegar, so that it would degrade swiftly and would not remain among them for long. It’s also said that Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras, whose book on theology is preserved, experienced a dream after 15 he arrived among the Lacedaemonians, and told the Lacedaemonian kings not to place value on money; and on the same night, it’s said that appeared to the other king, to trust Pherecydes; and as soon as Pherecydes woke up and spoke to the king, it’s said that their constitution changed course, when it was once again on the verge of declining into oligarchy.

165,1 After Socrates has criticised (elenxas) Alcibiades along these lines, with a long and drawn-out speech (because someone who presents history is obliged to use drawn-out speeches, since the discussion is about particular cases (merikôn), whereas in universal, discourse by question and answer is appropriate, because discussion through questioning is 5 appropriate to beings that are bodiless and partless, whereas drawn-out discussion befits bodies which have parts and are extended in space: that is also why orators use drawn-out speech, since they are concerned with particular cases) – after criticising him for the first part as ignorant of himself, at this point he begins the third part by saying, ‘No, my 10 excellent friend, trust in me and in the Delphic inscription, and “Know Thyself” ’ . In these words, with the god’s favour, the second part and the present survey are complete. Again, if you care to consider the wealth : Notice how disgusted Socrates is when he compares Alcibiades to the kings of the Persians 15 in terms of lifestyle (diaitan); this is also why he uses the words, ‘If you care to’. And he will appear even more disgusted later, when he compares him on the of wealth, because is even outside of us; this is also why, still disgusted, he says ‘we can’t leave this unspoken’ . Note, too, how Socrates chooses the right moment to speak like an orator and use a mocking tone, setting everything out in plurals instead of singular forms, using the words ‘wealths’ and ‘luxuries’. And he speaks about ‘trailing robes’ (using two words) because the Persians wear tunics that stretch to their feet, which is also why they’re called ‘robe-trailers’ (helkesipeploi); as do the Indians, like the Ionians too. The throng of servants-in-waiting: Notice as well how he introduces 166,1 plural forms to elevate , even though the train is singular. and

For this is also what the poet means when he says of the Trojans, ‘The Trojans with clamour’, etc. , whereas he says of the Greeks, ‘ silently, in fear of their commanders’ . And this is appropriate to self-control, that the inferior 15 obey the superior; for when develops in the remotest portion of the soul, it causes to obey reason. And their love of hardship, love of victory, and love of honour: For the Laconians were also fond of hardship (philoponoi), which is why from childhood they were whipped, habituating them for hard work; for they 20 received whippings from four years of age. But they also used to enjoy 167,1 practicing gymnastics at the Eurytus, as Euripides says, with men and women exercising together. For they have so much land of their own, and in Messene could compete with in size or excellence...]: Notice that he begins by comparing wealth; and he makes the comparison first on the basis of wealth moved by another (heterokinêtos). The Peloponnese was divided into five parts, of which one was Messene. Also, the language should be interpreted in reverse: ‘For they have so much land, both in size and excellence, of their 10 own and in Messene, that not one could compete with’. For many generations, have been pouring in to them from all over Greece: Note how it’s also possible to show from these words that Plato really reproaches , since it’s a sign of envy only to take and never to give. Notice, too, how he used this kind of talk to dismiss them as women: for love wealth because of their low birth and natural weakness. That’s also why the Persians have a feminine look, since they enjoy wearing that kind of jewellery. Now if someone were to say to , the king’s mother : He builds his speech up from the prior generation to the contemporary to the posterior, speaking of the king’s mother, wife, and daughter. And he remarks, ‘If someone were to tell that Alcibiades wishes to enter competition with her son, how in the world could you compete with 15 him with confidence? With these comments , then, he introduces the third part and he comes to the two refutations that he laid out in the two 5 parts : ‘No, my blessed friend, trust in me and in the Delphic inscription and “Know Thyself” ’ . And he calls ‘blessed’ (makarion) because he is about to link him to the gods; and in this context, ‘blessedness’ (makariotês) is used for the negation of ‘fatedness’ (kêr), since ma– indicates negation. And he positions himself before the god because he is the proximate cause of Alcibiades’ salvation. 10 By using the phrase ‘Know Thyself’ (gnôthi seauton), he reveals the content of command (prostattomenon), since he used the instruction to reveal what commanded: he used the word ‘know’ (gnôthi) that we are not a body (sôma) (for does not have knowledge), nor a combination (for this does not have knowledge either, insofar as it is a combination, since it certainly doesn’t have knowledge as a body), but we are a soul (psukhê), and not a vegetative soul (for that has no knowledge); and he used the word ‘thyself’ (seauton) since also not non-rational (alogos) (for the non-rational does not revert upon itself), but rational, and not always completely rational, but sometimes even ignorant. That’s also the reason why he added the command ‘know’ (gnôthi): for no one commands the agent to act, but now , he commands him to know himself.

20 ‘For you’re in urgent need of cultivation’, he says, ‘and you’re not the only one, but I am too. For all human beings – more than other animals – stand in need of 172,1 cultivation, and you and I especially so, most of all’. Now let us investigate why he maintains these three positions: that is, why is Socrates ignorant of himself? Why is the human being alone in need of cultivation, more than other animals? And why does the third point also hold, that Socrates and Alcibiades especially stand in need of cultivation, more so than other human beings?

Well then, the answer to the first question is that ‘self-knowledge’ is said in many ways (pollakhôs): it is possible to know oneself with respect to one’s external ; and of course it is possible to know oneself with respect to one’s body; and it is possible to know oneself as a civic or social person (politikôs), when one knows oneself in the tripartition of one’s soul; and it is possible to know oneself as a purificatory person (kathartikôs), when one knows oneself in the act of liberation from the affections (pathê); and it is possible to know oneself as a contemplative person (theôrêtikôs), when a person contemplates himself as liberated (heauton... theasêtai); it is 10 possible to know oneself theologically (theologikôs), when a person knows himself according to his paradigmatic Form (idea); and it is possible to know oneself as an inspired person (enthousiastikôs), when a person knows himself as a unity (kata to hen) and, thus bonded to his proper god (oikeios theos), acts with inspiration (enthousiâi). Now Socrates did not know himself as an inspired person, which is also why in the Phaedrus he says, ‘it is ridiculous to look into other things, while remaining ignorant of myself’ .

As for the second question, say that the human 15 being stands in need of cultivation more than other animals, not only with respect to his body (since nature made it naked, after providing hair all over for other animals, and horns for some, and hooves), and again not only with respect to externals (since we are the only animal to need shelter from houses), but also with respect to reason (logos), since the troubles that 20 human beings face are extremely harsh, more so than other animals, which is why we have resourceful reason within , like some Odysseus toiling to the limit for his appetite, and elaborating his sufferings (pathê). That is also why it was said,
The earth breeds nothing feebler than a human being.
173,1 For this reason, then, says that the human being is more in need of cultivation .

As for the third , why Alcibiades and Socrates more than other people: first, Alcibiades , because great natures become causes of great harm (kaka) when they go without cultivation, just as when they happen to be cultivated, they are the causes of great goods. As a matter 5 of fact, this is analogous to the case of rich land that produces good fruit when it is cultivated and farmed, but when it’s uncultivated, naturally produces thistles (for it knows only how to generate its produce, without distinguishing whether it is thorny or otherwise); that is just the situation with talented natures (dexiai phuseis). And wherever Alcibiades inclined from or to, he made a change (tropê). 10 For instance, when he joined the Laconians, he slept with the king’s wife, mother, and daughter; and when he came to Athens, he advised his guardian Pericles to consider how he might avoid rendering an account to the Athenians of the money spent on the Athena of Pheidias. That’s also why that man used to say to the people who came to examine the expenditures that ‘it was spent 15 on necessities (to deon)’. And the comedy about him says ‘I was ruined (apôlesa) on necessities’, instead of ‘I spent (anêlôsa)’. And that was the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. For these reasons, Alcibiades stood in need of a great deal of cultivation.

But Socrates was also because of the loftiness of his love of wisdom (philosophia). Alternatively, since he’s a lover he wants to be in the same state as his beloved, so he says that he is with him in 20 standing in need of much cultivation.

That is the survey. Trust in me and in the Delphic inscription: He allies himself with the god: 174,1 and he has many grounds for doing so. Thus in the Phaedrus he calls himself ‘a fellow-slave of the swans’; so too in the present dialogue he allied himself with Apollo, criticising the Lacedaemonians for their love of money (for the oracle was given about them:

For just as each skill has knowledge of one thing, but is ignorant of many , while the philosopher knows all beings, so too whereas each of the other skills has a single underlying and deliberates carefully about it, the civic (politikê ) takes all beings as its practical materials (prakta), with a view to improving them. Now the form (eidos) of political knowledge is rulership (arkhein); and it’s not the rulership of non-rational , ‘caring by blows’, but of human beings; and it’s not of human beings simply, since the doctor also rules human beings in distress; nor of human beings when they reap (for that’s the 20 work of farming); nor of sailors (for that’s the pilot’s work); nor of singers (for that’s the chorus-teacher’s work); but of human beings ‘as they deal with (khrômenôn) human beings’ . But since the pilot also rules people who are boatswains (it’s people who look after the ship’s tackle who are called 179,1 ‘boatswains’), who rule the people who row, and the chorus-teacher rules the flute-players who lead the singers, therefore adds that the statesman rules human beings, those who are in positions of leadership, and who join together in contractual agreements.
5 And the efficient cause (poiêtikon aition) is not wisdom (sophia), but practical wisdom (phronêsis), which is concerned with practical matters (prakta).

And the statesman’s final is producing agreement and affection in the state (polis), either between understandings (gnôseis), in which case he produces agreement (homonoia) (for agreement is nothing but commonality of understandings and shared belief (homodoxia)), or between ways of life, in which case he produces affection (storgê) (for <affection> is natural love (philia)). Now these two are not identical, since there is such a thing as affection without agreement, as for instance a husband and wife love one another without agreeing (for they are not in agreement in their domains of expertise: the woman, for example, is not in agreement with her husband on matters of war or expertise in armed combat, while the man with his wife in knowledge of wool-spinning); and conversely, there is agreement without affection, since potters agree , out of their concern for the same objects of knowledge, and they have the same thoughts (ta auta noousi) (for this is called ‘agreement’ (homonoia)), yet they do not have affection for one another, whence the saying
20 One potter begrudges another; likewise for the carpenter.

180,1 Now how might the statesman produce agreement and affection in the state? He could produce affection, if he causes the citizens to be disposed to one another like a state comprised of a single family, so that they measure their 5 kinship by age, regarding all the aged as fathers, those who are much smaller as children, their contemporaries as brothers, so that instead of his saying ‘age-mate delights age-mate’, we should say ‘citizen delights citizen’. And if everyone were to enjoy the same experiences of sight and sound, agreement follows. For agreement was a shared understanding (koinônia gnôseôn); and those who have achieved this would have a shared vision and hearing, since the senses are kinds of understanding.

10 And that is the survey. Tell me: we say that we want to become as good as possible? 15 Since Alcibiades was describing friendship as the goal of the statesman’s knowledge, Socrates challenges him – not because he himself disagrees that friendship is the goal, but because he suspected that Alcibiades did not distinguish between affection (storgê) and friendship (philia). And he 20 shows that agreement is friendship both directly, and by an argument from impossibility . His direct runs as follows: ‘If disagreement is enmity, agreement will be friendship; therefore, not only is affection (storgê) friendship, but so is agreement’. And his argument 184,1 from impossibility runs as follows: ‘If a husband and wife do not agree, and if we were claiming that agreement is to know the same things, but these people <do not> know the same things (, since supposes that he need know nothing of wool-spinning, and thinks that she need know nothing about mastering horses); but those who do not enjoy the same objects of knowledge are not friends to one another; therefore, 5 a husband and wife are not friends to one another’. (And it’s clear that they are not in agreement with respect to their immediate goal, inasmuch as one happens to understand horsemanship, the other wool-spinning, whereas they are in agreement with respect to their more final goal, for the goes to war to protect his wife – because ‘for their children and for their wives’ – but she weaves wool to protect the man, so that he may not be 10 destroyed by the onslaught of the climate).

Next, having extracted from that those who do not enjoy the same objects of knowledge are not friends to one another, he proves that just people are not able to organise (oikein) their cities well.
